Cease to persuade, my loving Proteus. / Home-keeping youth have ever homely wits. / Were't not affection chains thy tender days / To the sweet glances of thy honoured love, / I rather would entreat thy company / To see the wonders of the world abroad / Than, living dully sluggardized at home, / Wear out thy youth with shapeless idleness. / But since thou lov'st, love still, and thrive therein, / Even as I would when I to love begin.

Stop trying to talk me round, my dear Proteus. Young men who stay at home always have small-town minds. If love didn't tie your young life to the sweet looks of the girl you adore, I'd rather beg you to come with me and see the wonders of the world than watch you stay at home, dull and lazy, wasting your youth in aimless idleness. But since you are in love, keep loving, and may it go well for you, as I'd hope it would for me if I ever start.

Wilt thou be gone? Sweet Valentine, adieu. / Think on thy Proteus when thou haply seest / Some rare noteworthy object in thy travel. / Wish me partaker in thy happiness / When thou dost meet good hap; and in thy danger, / If ever danger do environ thee, / Commend thy grievance to my holy prayers, / For I will be thy beadsman, Valentine.

Are you really going? Sweet Valentine, goodbye. Think of your Proteus whenever you happen to see something rare and remarkable on your travels. Wish I could share your happiness when good luck comes your way; and if you're ever in danger, hand your troubles over to my prayers, because I'll pray for you, Valentine.
And on a love-book pray for my success?
Praying for my success on a book of love poems, I suppose?
Upon some book I love I'll pray for thee.
I'll pray for you on some book I love.
That's on some shallow story of deep love, / How young Leander crossed the Hellespont.
That'll be some shallow story about deep love, like young Leander swimming the Hellespont.
That's a deep story of a deeper love, / For he was more than over shoes in love.
That's a deep story about an even deeper love, because he was in love over his shoes, right up to the neck.
'Tis true; for you are over boots in love, / And yet you never swam the Hellespont.
True; and you are in love over your boots, and yet you've never swum the Hellespont.
Over the boots? Nay, give me not the boots.
Over my boots? No, don't mock me.
No, I will not, for it boots thee not.
No, I won't, because it would do you no good.

To be in love, where scorn is bought with groans, / Coy looks with heart-sore sighs, one fading moment's mirth / With twenty watchful, weary, tedious nights. / If haply won, perhaps a hapless gain; / If lost, why then a grievous labour won; / However, but a folly bought with wit, / Or else a wit by folly vanquished.

Being in love, where you buy scorn with groans, a coy look with heart-sick sighs, one brief moment of happiness with twenty sleepless, weary, endless nights. If you happen to win, it may be an unlucky prize; if you lose, all you've won is misery. Either way, it's foolishness bought with your intelligence, or intelligence beaten by foolishness.
So, by your circumstance, you call me fool.
So by that argument you're calling me a fool.
So, by your circumstance, I fear you'll prove.
By the way you're going, I'm afraid you'll turn out to be one.
'Tis love you cavil at. I am not Love.
It's love you're finding fault with. I'm not Love.
Love is your master, for he masters you; / And he that is so yoked by a fool / Methinks should not be chronicled for wise.
Love is your master, because he controls you; and anyone yoked to a fool like that shouldn't go down in history as wise.
Yet writers say, as in the sweetest bud / The eating canker dwells, so eating love / Inhabits in the finest wits of all.
Yet writers say that just as the grub that eats a flower lives in the sweetest bud, so love, which eats away at us, lives in the finest minds of all.

And writers say, as the most forward bud / Is eaten by the canker ere it blow, / Even so by love the young and tender wit / Is turned to folly, blasting in the bud, / Losing his verdure even in the prime, / And all the fair effects of future hopes. / But wherefore waste I time to counsel thee / That art a votary to fond desire? / Once more adieu. My father at the road / Expects my coming, there to see me shipped.

And writers also say that just as the earliest bud is eaten by the grub before it can open, so love turns a young, tender mind to foolishness. It withers in the bud, losing its freshness in its prime and all the good things it promised for the future. But why am I wasting my time advising you, when you're devoted to foolish desire? Once more, goodbye. My father is waiting at the harbour to see me off on the ship.
And thither will I bring thee, Valentine.
And I'll go there with you, Valentine.

Sweet Proteus, no. Now let us take our leave. / To Milan let me hear from thee by letters / Of thy success in love, and what news else / Betideth here in absence of thy friend; / And I likewise will visit thee with mine.
No, sweet Proteus. Let's say goodbye here. Write to me in Milan about how your love goes and whatever else happens here while your friend is away, and I'll write back in the same way.
All happiness bechance to thee in Milan.
I wish you every happiness in Milan.
As much to you at home, and so farewell.
The same to you at home. And so, goodbye.

He after honour hunts, I after love. / He leaves his friends to dignify them more; / I leave myself, my friends, and all for love. / Thou, Julia, thou hast metamorphosed me, / Made me neglect my studies, lose my time, / War with good counsel, set the world at nought; / Made wit with musing weak, heart sick with thought.

He hunts for honour, I hunt for love. He leaves his friends to bring them more credit; I leave myself, my friends and everything for love. You, Julia, you have transformed me. You've made me neglect my studies, waste my time, fight against good advice and care nothing for the world. You've made my mind weak with daydreaming and my heart sick with worry.
Sir Proteus, 'save you. Saw you my master?
Sir Proteus, God save you. Have you seen my master?
But now he parted hence to embark for Milan.
He's just left here to board the ship for Milan.
Twenty to one, then, he is shipped already, / And I have played the sheep in losing him.
Then twenty to one he's already on board, and I've been a sheep and lost him.
Indeed a sheep doth very often stray, / An if the shepherd be a while away.
Well, a sheep often does stray if the shepherd is away for a while.
You conclude that my master is a shepherd then, and I a sheep?
So you're saying my master is a shepherd and I'm a sheep?
Why then, my horns are his horns, whether I wake or sleep.
Then my horns are his horns, whether I'm awake or asleep.
A silly answer, and fitting well a sheep.
A silly answer, and just right for a sheep.
This proves me still a sheep.
That proves I'm still a sheep.
True, and thy master a shepherd.
True, and your master is a shepherd.
Nay, that I can deny by a circumstance.
No, I can disprove that with an argument.
It shall go hard but I'll prove it by another.
It'll go hard if I can't prove it with another.
The shepherd seeks the sheep, and not the sheep the shepherd; but I / seek my master, and my master seeks not me. Therefore I am no sheep.
The shepherd looks for the sheep, not the sheep for the shepherd. But I look for my master, and my master doesn't look for me. So I'm not a sheep.
The sheep for fodder follow the shepherd; the shepherd for food follows / not the sheep. Thou for wages followest thy master; thy master for / wages follows not thee. Therefore thou art a sheep.
The sheep follows the shepherd for food; the shepherd doesn't follow the sheep for food. You follow your master for wages; your master doesn't follow you for wages. So you are a sheep.
Such another proof will make me cry "baa".
One more proof like that and I'll be bleating "baa".
But dost thou hear? Gav'st thou my letter to Julia?
But listen, did you give my letter to Julia?
Ay, sir. I, a lost mutton, gave your letter to her, a laced mutton, and / she, a laced mutton, gave me, a lost mutton, nothing for my labour.
Yes, sir. I, a lost sheep, gave your letter to her, a fancy lady in a laced bodice, and she, the fancy lady, gave me, the lost sheep, nothing for my trouble.
Here's too small a pasture for such store of muttons.
There's too little pasture here for so many sheep.
If the ground be overcharged, you were best stick her.
If the field's overstocked, you'd better slaughter her.
Nay, in that you are astray; 'twere best pound you.
No, you've gone astray there; it would be better to pen you up in a pound.
Nay, sir, less than a pound shall serve me for carrying your letter.
No, sir, less than a pound will do me as payment for carrying your letter.
You mistake; I mean the pound, a pinfold.
You've got it wrong. I mean a pound for animals, a pinfold.
From a pound to a pin? Fold it over and over, / 'Tis threefold too little for carrying a letter to your lover.
From a pound to a pin? Fold it over and over, and it's still three times too little for carrying a letter to your lover.
A nod and "Ay": that makes "noddy", a fool.
You mistook, sir. I say she did nod, and you ask me if she did nod; and / I say "Ay".
You've got it wrong, sir. I say she did nod, and you ask me if she nodded, and I say "Ay".
Now you have taken the pains to set it together, take it for your / pains.
Well, since you've taken the trouble to put it together, keep it for your trouble.
No, no, you shall have it for bearing the letter.
No, no, you can have it for carrying the letter.
Well, I perceive I must be fain to bear with you.
Well, I see I'll just have to put up with you.
Why, sir, how do you bear with me?
Why, sir, how are you putting up with me?
Marry, sir, the letter, very orderly, having nothing but the word / "noddy" for my pains.
Well, sir, by carrying the letter properly and getting nothing but the word "noddy" for my trouble.
Beshrew me, but you have a quick wit.
And yet it cannot overtake your slow purse.
And yet my wit can't catch up with your slow purse.
Come, come, open the matter; in brief, what said she?
Come on, come on, out with it. In short, what did she say?
Open your purse, that the money and the matter may be both at once / delivered.
Open your purse, so that the money and the news can be handed over at the same time.
[Giving him a coin] Well, sir, here is for your pains. What said / she?
[Giving him a coin] Well, sir, here's something for your trouble. What did she say?
Truly, sir, I think you'll hardly win her.
Honestly, sir, I don't think you'll win her easily.
Why? Couldst thou perceive so much from her?
Why? Could you tell that much from her?

Sir, I could perceive nothing at all from her; no, not so much as a / ducat for delivering your letter. And being so hard to me that brought / your mind, I fear she'll prove as hard to you in telling your mind. / Give her no token but stones, for she's as hard as steel.

Sir, I couldn't get anything from her at all, not even a ducat for delivering your letter. And since she was so hard on me for bringing your feelings to her, I'm afraid she'll be just as hard on you when you tell her them in person. Don't give her any gifts but stones, because she's as hard as steel.

No, not so much as "Take this for thy pains." To testify your bounty, I / thank you, you have testerned me; in requital whereof, henceforth carry / your letters yourself. And so, sir, I'll commend you to my master.

No, not even "Take this for your trouble." To show how generous you are, thank you for tipping me sixpence. In return, from now on carry your letters yourself. And so, sir, I'll go and give my master your regards.
Go, go, begone, to save your ship from wrack, / Which cannot perish having thee aboard, / Being destined to a drier death on shore.
Go on, go, be off and save your ship from being wrecked. It can't sink with you on board, because you're destined to die a drier death on land, by hanging.
I must go send some better messenger. / I fear my Julia would not deign my lines, / Receiving them from such a worthless post.
I'll have to send a better messenger. I'm afraid my Julia wouldn't accept my letters from such a worthless postman.
But say, Lucetta, now we are alone, / Wouldst thou then counsel me to fall in love?
But tell me, Lucetta, now that we're alone, would you advise me to fall in love?
Ay, madam, so you stumble not unheedfully.
Yes, madam, as long as you don't stumble into it carelessly.
Of all the fair resort of gentlemen / That every day with parle encounter me, / In thy opinion which is worthiest love?
Of all the fine gentlemen who come every day to talk with me, which do you think most deserves my love?
Please you, repeat their names, I'll show my mind / According to my shallow simple skill.
If you'll repeat their names, I'll give you my opinion, as far as my small, simple judgement goes.
What think'st thou of the fair Sir Eglamour?
What do you think of the handsome Sir Eglamour?
As of a knight well-spoken, neat, and fine; / But, were I you, he never should be mine.
That he's a well-spoken knight, neat and elegant; but if I were you, he'd never be mine.
What think'st thou of the rich Mercatio?
What do you think of the rich Mercatio?
Well of his wealth; but of himself, so-so.
I think well of his money, but of the man himself, so-so.
What think'st thou of the gentle Proteus?
What do you think of the gentle Proteus?
Lord, Lord, to see what folly reigns in us!
Lord, Lord, what fools we all are!
How now? What means this passion at his name?
What's this? Why such a reaction at his name?
Pardon, dear madam, 'tis a passing shame / That I, unworthy body as I am, / Should censure thus on lovely gentlemen.
Forgive me, dear madam. It's a real shame that someone as lowly as I am should pass judgement like this on fine gentlemen.
Why not on Proteus, as of all the rest?
Why not on Proteus, as well as all the others?
Then thus: of many good I think him best.
Then here it is: of many good men, I think he's the best.
I have no other but a woman's reason: / I think him so because I think him so.
I have no reason but a woman's reason: I think so because I think so.
And wouldst thou have me cast my love on him?
And would you have me give my love to him?
Ay, if you thought your love not cast away.
Yes, as long as you didn't think your love was being thrown away.
Why, he of all the rest hath never moved me.
But of all of them, he's the only one who has never tried to win me.
Yet he of all the rest I think best loves ye.
Yet of all of them, I think he loves you best.
His little speaking shows his love but small.
He says so little, which shows his love is small.
Fire that's closest kept burns most of all.
The fire that's most shut in burns hottest.
They do not love that do not show their love.
People who don't show their love don't love.
O, they love least that let men know their love.
Oh, the ones who let everyone know they're in love love least.
I would I knew his mind.
I wish I knew what he thought.
"To Julia." Tell me, who is it from?
The letter will tell you that.
Say, say, who gave it thee?
Tell me, tell me, who gave it to you?
Sir Valentine's page, and sent, I think, from Proteus. / He would have given it you, but I, being in the way, / Did in your name receive it. Pardon the fault, I pray.
Sir Valentine's servant, and sent, I think, by Proteus. He would have given it to you, but I happened to meet him and took it in your name. Please forgive me for doing so.

Now, by my modesty, a goodly broker! / Dare you presume to harbour wanton lines? / To whisper and conspire against my youth? / Now trust me, 'tis an office of great worth, / And you an officer fit for the place. / There, take the paper; see it be returned, / Or else return no more into my sight.

Upon my honour, what a fine go-between you are! How dare you take in love letters? Whispering and plotting against my innocence? Believe me, that's a very respectable job, and you're just the right person for it. There, take the letter back and see it's returned, or never come into my sight again.
To plead for love deserves more fee than hate.
Pleading for love deserves a better reward than hate.
Yes, so you can think it over.

And yet I would I had o'erlooked the letter. / It were a shame to call her back again / And pray her to a fault for which I chid her. / What fool is she, that knows I am a maid / And would not force the letter to my view, / Since maids in modesty say "No" to that / Which they would have the profferer construe "Ay". / Fie, fie, how wayward is this foolish love / That like a testy babe will scratch the nurse / And presently, all humbled, kiss the rod! / How churlishly I chid Lucetta hence, / When willingly I would have had her here! / How angerly I taught my brow to frown, / When inward joy enforced my heart to smile! / My penance is to call Lucetta back / And ask remission for my folly past. / What ho! Lucetta!

And yet I wish I'd read the letter. It would be embarrassing to call her back and beg her to do the very thing I scolded her for. What a fool she is! She knows I'm a girl, so why didn't she force me to read it? Girls say "no", out of modesty, to things they want the person offering to take as "yes". Honestly, how contrary this foolish love is! Like a bad-tempered baby, it scratches the nurse and then, all meek, kisses the stick it was smacked with. How rudely I drove Lucetta away, when I really wanted her to stay! How angrily I made myself frown, when inside I was so happy I wanted to smile! My punishment will be to call Lucetta back and ask forgiveness for my silliness. Hello there! Lucetta!
I would it were, / That you might kill your stomach on your meat / And not upon your maid.
I wish it were, so you could take out your temper on your food and not on your maid.
What is't that you took up so gingerly?
What's that you picked up so carefully?
Then why did you bend down?
To take a paper up that I let fall.
To pick up a piece of paper I dropped.
Then let it lie for those that it concerns.
Then leave it lying there for the people it does concern.
Madam, it will not lie where it concerns, / Unless it have a false interpreter.
Madam, it won't lie about the person it concerns, unless someone misreads it.
Some love of yours hath writ to you in rhyme.
Some lover of yours has written to you in verse.
That I might sing it, madam, to a tune. / Give me a note. Your ladyship can set—
So that I could sing it to a tune, madam. Give me a note. Your ladyship can set—
As little by such toys as may be possible. / Best sing it to the tune of "Light o' Love".
As little store by such trifles as possible. You'd better sing it to the tune of "Light o' Love".
It is too heavy for so light a tune.
It's too heavy for such a light tune.
Heavy? Belike it hath some burden then?
Heavy? Then I suppose it has a weighty refrain?
Ay, and melodious were it, would you sing it.
Yes, and it would sound lovely if you sang it.
Let's see your song. [Taking the letter] / How now, minion!
Let me see your song. [Taking the letter] What's this, you hussy!
Keep tune there still, so you will sing it out. / And yet methinks I do not like this tune.
Keep to that tune and you'll sing it to the end. And yet I don't think I like this tune.
No, madam, it is too sharp.
And you, girl, are too cheeky.
Nay, now you are too flat / And mar the concord with too harsh a descant. / There wanteth but a mean to fill your song.
No, now you're too flat, and you spoil the harmony with such a harsh line. All your song needs is a middle part, a tenor, to fill it out.
The mean is drowned with your unruly bass.
The middle part is drowned out by your unruly bass.
Indeed, I bid the base for Proteus.
Well, I'm speaking up for Proteus.
This babble shall not henceforth trouble me. / Here is a coil with protestation! [Tears the letter] / Go, get you gone, and let the papers lie. / You would be fingering them to anger me.
This chatter won't bother me any more. What a fuss about a love letter! [Tears the letter] Go on, get out, and leave the papers lying there. You'd fiddle with them just to annoy me.
She makes it strange, but she would be best pleased / To be so angered with another letter.
She's acting distant, but she'd be delighted to be made this angry by another letter.

Nay, would I were so angered with the same! / O hateful hands, to tear such loving words! / Injurious wasps, to feed on such sweet honey / And kill the bees that yield it with your stings! / I'll kiss each several paper for amends. / Look, here is writ kind Julia. Unkind Julia! / As in revenge of thy ingratitude, / I throw thy name against the bruising stones, / Trampling contemptuously on thy disdain. / And here is writ love-wounded Proteus. / Poor wounded name, my bosom as a bed / Shall lodge thee till thy wound be throughly healed; / And thus I search it with a sovereign kiss. / But twice or thrice was Proteus written down. / Be calm, good wind, blow not a word away / Till I have found each letter in the letter / Except mine own name. That some whirlwind bear / Unto a ragged, fearful, hanging rock, / And throw it thence into the raging sea. / Lo, here in one line is his name twice writ: / Poor forlorn Proteus, passionate Proteus, / To the sweet Julia. That I'll tear away; / And yet I will not, sith so prettily / He couples it to his complaining names. / Thus will I fold them one upon another. / Now kiss, embrace, contend, do what you will.

No, I wish I were angry with this same one! Oh, hateful hands, to tear up such loving words! Spiteful wasps, to feed on such sweet honey and kill the bees that make it with your stings! I'll kiss each scrap of paper to make up for it. Look, here it says "kind Julia". Unkind Julia! To punish you for being so ungrateful, I'll throw your name against the hard stones and trample on your scorn. And here it says "love-wounded Proteus". Poor wounded name, my breast will be your bed until your wound is fully healed, and I'll treat it with a healing kiss. But "Proteus" was written two or three times. Be calm, good wind, don't blow away a single word until I've found every letter in the letter, except my own name. Let a whirlwind carry that off to a jagged, terrifying, overhanging rock and throw it from there into the raging sea. Look, here's his name twice in one line: "Poor forlorn Proteus, passionate Proteus, to the sweet Julia." I'll tear that part off. And yet I won't, since he joins it so prettily to his own sad names. I'll fold them one on top of the other like this. Now kiss, embrace, wrestle, do whatever you like.
Madam, dinner is ready, and your father stays.
Madam, dinner is ready, and your father is waiting.
What, shall these papers lie like tell-tales here?
What, are you going to leave these papers lying here to tell tales?
If you respect them, best to take them up.
If you care about them, you'd better pick them up.
Nay, I was taken up for laying them down. / Yet here they shall not lie, for catching cold.
No, I was told off for putting them down. But they mustn't lie here and catch cold.
I see you have a month's mind to them.
I can see you have a real hankering for them.
Ay, madam, you may say what sights you see; / I see things too, although you judge I wink.
Yes, madam, you can say whatever you think you see. I see things too, though you think I'm turning a blind eye.
Come, come, will't please you go?
Come on, come on, will you come?
Tell me, Pantino, what sad talk was that / Wherewith my brother held you in the cloister?
Tell me, Pantino, what was that serious talk my brother was having with you in the cloister?
'Twas of his nephew Proteus, your son.
It was about his nephew Proteus, your son.

He wondered that your lordship / Would suffer him to spend his youth at home / While other men, of slender reputation, / Put forth their sons to seek preferment out: / Some to the wars to try their fortune there; / Some to discover islands far away; / Some to the studious universities. / For any or for all these exercises / He said that Proteus your son was meet, / And did request me to importune you / To let him spend his time no more at home, / Which would be great impeachment to his age / In having known no travel in his youth.

He wondered why your lordship lets him spend his youth at home, while other men of much lower standing send their sons out to make their way in the world: some to the wars, to try their luck there; some to discover islands far away; some to the universities to study. He said your son Proteus was fit for any or all of these, and he asked me to urge you not to let him stay at home any longer. It would be a great disadvantage to him when he's older if he'd never travelled when young.

Nor need'st thou much importune me to that / Whereon this month I have been hammering. / I have considered well his loss of time, / And how he cannot be a perfect man, / Not being tried and tutored in the world. / Experience is by industry achieved / And perfected by the swift course of time. / Then tell me whither were I best to send him?

You don't need to urge me much about that. I've been turning it over all month. I've thought hard about how he's wasting his time, and how he can't become a complete man without being tested and taught by the world. Experience is gained by hard work and perfected by the passing of time. So tell me, where would be best to send him?
I think your lordship is not ignorant / How his companion, youthful Valentine, / Attends the Emperor in his royal court.
I think your lordship knows that his friend, young Valentine, is serving the Emperor at his royal court.

'Twere good, I think, your lordship sent him thither. / There shall he practise tilts and tournaments, / Hear sweet discourse, converse with noblemen, / And be in eye of every exercise / Worthy his youth and nobleness of birth.

I think it would be good if your lordship sent him there. He could practise jousting and tournaments, hear fine conversation, mix with noblemen, and see every activity fit for a young man of his noble birth.

I like thy counsel; well hast thou advised, / And that thou mayst perceive how well I like it, / The execution of it shall make known. / Even with the speediest expedition / I will dispatch him to the Emperor's court.
I like your advice; you've advised me well. And to show you how much I like it, I'll act on it. I'll send him to the Emperor's court as fast as possible.
Tomorrow, may it please you, Don Alphonso / With other gentlemen of good esteem / Are journeying to salute the Emperor / And to commend their service to his will.
Tomorrow, if it suits you, Don Alphonso and some other well-respected gentlemen are travelling to pay their respects to the Emperor and offer him their service.
Good company. With them shall Proteus go.
Good company. Proteus will go with them.
And in good time! Now will we break with him.
And just at the right moment! Now we'll tell him.

Sweet love, sweet lines, sweet life! / Here is her hand, the agent of her heart; / Here is her oath for love, her honour's pawn. / O, that our fathers would applaud our loves / To seal our happiness with their consents. / O heavenly Julia!

Sweet love, sweet words, sweet life! Here is her handwriting, which speaks for her heart; here is her vow of love, which she pledges on her honour. Oh, if only our fathers would approve of our love and seal our happiness with their consent. Oh, heavenly Julia!
How now? What letter are you reading there?
What's this? What letter are you reading there?
May't please your lordship, 'tis a word or two / Of commendations sent from Valentine, / Delivered by a friend that came from him.
If it please your lordship, it's a few lines of greetings from Valentine, brought by a friend who came from him.
Lend me the letter. Let me see what news.
Let me have the letter. Let me see the news.
There is no news, my lord, but that he writes / How happily he lives, how well beloved / And daily graced by the Emperor, / Wishing me with him, partner of his fortune.
There's no news, my lord, except that he writes about how happily he's living, how well loved he is and how the Emperor favours him every day. He wishes I were with him, to share his good fortune.
And how stand you affected to his wish?
And how do you feel about his wish?
As one relying on your lordship's will, / And not depending on his friendly wish.
As someone who depends on your lordship's wishes, not on his friendly one.

My will is something sorted with his wish. / Muse not that I thus suddenly proceed, / For what I will, I will, and there an end. / I am resolved that thou shalt spend some time / With Valentinus in the Emperor's court. / What maintenance he from his friends receives, / Like exhibition thou shalt have from me. / Tomorrow be in readiness to go. / Excuse it not, for I am peremptory.

My wishes rather agree with his. Don't be surprised that I'm acting so suddenly, because what I want, I want, and that's the end of it. I've decided that you'll spend some time with Valentine at the Emperor's court. Whatever allowance his family gives him, you'll have the same from me. Be ready to leave tomorrow. Don't make excuses, because my mind is made up.
My lord, I cannot be so soon provided; / Please you deliberate a day or two.
My lord, I can't get ready so soon. Please think about it for a day or two.
Look what thou want'st shall be sent after thee. / No more of stay. Tomorrow thou must go. / Come on, Pantino, you shall be employed / To hasten on his expedition.
Whatever you need will be sent after you. No more delay. You must go tomorrow. Come on, Pantino, you'll be put to work hurrying on his departure.

Thus have I shunned the fire for fear of burning / And drenched me in the sea, where I am drowned. / I feared to show my father Julia's letter / Lest he should take exceptions to my love, / And with the vantage of mine own excuse / Hath he excepted most against my love. / O, how this spring of love resembleth / The uncertain glory of an April day, / Which now shows all the beauty of the sun, / And by an by a cloud takes all away.

So I've avoided the fire for fear of being burned, and jumped into the sea, where I'm drowning. I was afraid to show my father Julia's letter in case he objected to my love, and he has used my own excuse against me and done the most damage to my love. Oh, how this springtime of love is like the changeable glory of an April day, which one moment shows all the beauty of the sun, and the next a cloud takes it all away.
Sir Proteus, your father calls for you. / He is in haste. Therefore, I pray you, go.
Sir Proteus, your father is calling for you. He's in a hurry, so please go.
Why, this it is: my heart accords thereto, / And yet a thousand times it answers "No".
Well, that's how it is: my heart agrees to go, and yet a thousand times it says "No".
Not mine. My gloves are on.
Not mine. My gloves are on.
Why, then, this may be yours, for this is but one.
Well then, this could be yours, because it's only one.
Ha? Let me see. Ay, give it me, it's mine. / Sweet ornament that decks a thing divine! / Ah, Silvia, Silvia!
What? Let me see. Yes, give it to me, it's mine. Sweet ornament that adorns a heavenly thing! Ah, Silvia, Silvia!
She is not within hearing, sir.
Why, sir, who bade you call her?
Why, sir, who told you to call her?
Your worship, sir, or else I mistook.
Your worship did, sir, unless I misunderstood.
Well, you'll still be too forward.
And yet I was last chidden for being too slow.
And yet last time I was told off for being too slow.
Go to, sir. Tell me, do you know Madam Silvia?
That's enough, sir. Tell me, do you know Madam Silvia?
Why, how know you that I am in love?
Why, how do you know I'm in love?

Marry, by these special marks: first, you have learned, like Sir / Proteus, to wreathe your arms like a malcontent; to relish a love-song, / like a robin redbreast; to walk alone, like one that had the / pestilence; to sigh, like a schoolboy that had lost his ABC; to weep, / like a young wench that had buried her grandam; to fast, like one that / takes diet; to watch, like one that fears robbing; to speak puling, / like a beggar at Hallowmas. You were wont, when you laughed, to crow / like a cock; when you walked, to walk like one of the lions; when you / fasted, it was presently after dinner; when you looked sadly, it was / for want of money. And now you are metamorphosed with a mistress, that, / when I look on you, I can hardly think you my master.

Well, by these special signs. First, you've learned, like Sir Proteus, to fold your arms like a gloomy malcontent; to enjoy a love song, like a robin redbreast; to walk alone, like someone with the plague; to sigh, like a schoolboy who's lost his alphabet book; to weep, like a young girl who's buried her grandmother; to fast, like someone on a diet; to stay up all night, like someone afraid of burglars; to whine, like a beggar on All Saints' Day. You used to crow like a cockerel when you laughed, and swagger like a lion when you walked. When you fasted, it was right after dinner; when you looked sad, it was because you were short of money. And now a mistress has transformed you so much that when I look at you, I can hardly believe you're my master.
Are all these things perceived in me?
Can people see all these things in me?
They are all perceived without ye.
They can all be seen from outside you.

Without you? Nay, that's certain, for without you were so simple, none / else would. But you are so without these follies, that these follies / are within you, and shine through you like the water in an urinal, that / not an eye that sees you but is a physician to comment on your malady.

Outside you? No, that's certain, because no one but you would be so foolish. But you are so wrapped in these follies that they're inside you and shine through you, like urine in a doctor's glass, so that everyone who sees you becomes a doctor and diagnoses your illness.
But tell me, dost thou know my lady Silvia?
But tell me, do you know my lady Silvia?
She that you gaze on so as she sits at supper?
The one you stare at like that while she's sitting at supper?
Hast thou observed that? Even she I mean.
Have you noticed that? Yes, she's the one I mean.
Why, sir, I know her not.
Why, sir, I don't know her.
Dost thou know her by my gazing on her, and yet know'st her not?
You know her from my staring at her, and yet you don't know her?
Not so fair, boy, as well-favoured.
She's not so much beautiful, boy, as gracious.
Sir, I know that well enough.
Sir, I know that well enough.
That she is not so fair as, of you, well-favoured.
That she's not as beautiful as you think she's gracious.
I mean that her beauty is exquisite but her favour infinite.
I mean her beauty is exquisite, but her grace is infinite.
That's because the one is painted, and the other out of all count.
That's because one is painted on, and the other is beyond all counting.
How painted? And how out of count?
What do you mean, painted? And beyond counting?
Marry, sir, so painted to make her fair, that no man counts of her / beauty.
Well, sir, she's so painted with make-up to make her beautiful that no man takes her beauty into account.
How esteem'st thou me? I account of her beauty.
What do you take me for? I value her beauty.
You never saw her since she was deformed.
You've never seen her since she was disfigured.
How long hath she been deformed?
How long has she been disfigured?
Ever since you fell in love with her.
I have loved her ever since I saw her, and still I see her beautiful.
I've loved her ever since I first saw her, and I still see her as beautiful.
If you love her, you cannot see her.
If you love her, you can't see her.
Because Love is blind. O, that you had mine eyes, or your own eyes had / the lights they were wont to have when you chid at Sir Proteus for / going ungartered!
Because Love is blind. Oh, I wish you had my eyes, or that your own eyes were as clear as they were when you used to tell Sir Proteus off for going around with his stockings ungartered!
Your own present folly and her passing deformity; for he, being in / love, could not see to garter his hose; and you, being in love, cannot / see to put on your hose.
Your own present foolishness and her extreme ugliness. Because he, being in love, couldn't see to tie up his stockings; and you, being in love, can't see to put yours on.
Belike, boy, then you are in love, for last morning you could not see / to wipe my shoes.
Then I suppose you're in love, boy, because yesterday morning you couldn't see to clean my shoes.
True, sir, I was in love with my bed. I thank you, you swinged me for / my love, which makes me the bolder to chide you for yours.
True, sir, I was in love with my bed. Thank you for beating me for my love; it makes me bolder about telling you off for yours.
In conclusion, I stand affected to her.
In short, I am in love with her.
I would you were set, so your affection would cease.
I wish you'd sit down, so your affection would stop.
Last night she enjoined me to write some lines to one she loves.
Last night she asked me to write some lines to someone she loves.
No, boy, but as well as I can do them. / Peace, here she comes.
No, boy, they're as good as I can make them. Quiet, here she comes.
[Aside] O excellent motion! O exceeding puppet! / Now will he interpret to her.
[Aside] Oh, what a great puppet show! Oh, what a lovely puppet! Now he'll speak her lines for her.
Madam and mistress, a thousand good-morrows.
Madam and mistress, a thousand good mornings.
[Aside] O, give ye good e'en! Here's a million of manners.
[Aside] Oh, why not good evening too! Here's a million manners.
Sir Valentine and servant, to you two thousand.
Sir Valentine, my servant, two thousand to you.
[Aside] He should give her interest, and she gives it him.
[Aside] He ought to pay her the interest, and she's paying it to him.
As you enjoined me, I have writ your letter / Unto the secret nameless friend of yours, / Which I was much unwilling to proceed in / But for my duty to your ladyship.
As you asked me, I've written your letter to your secret, nameless friend. I was very unwilling to do it, except for my duty to your ladyship.
I thank you, gentle servant, 'tis very clerkly done.
Thank you, gentle servant. It's very skilfully done.
Now trust me, madam, it came hardly off, / For, being ignorant to whom it goes, / I writ at random, very doubtfully.
Believe me, madam, it was hard to do, because not knowing who it's going to, I wrote at random, very uncertainly.
Perchance you think too much of so much pains?
Perhaps you think it was too much trouble?
No, madam; so it stead you, I will write, / Please you command, a thousand times as much. / And yet—
No, madam. If it helps you, I'll write a thousand times as much, if you order me to. And yet—
A pretty period. Well, I guess the sequel; / And yet I will not name it. And yet I care not. / And yet take this again.
A nice place to stop. Well, I can guess what follows, and yet I won't say it. And yet I don't care. And yet, take this back.
And yet I thank you, / Meaning henceforth to trouble you no more.
And yet I thank you, though I mean not to trouble you again.
[Aside] And yet you will; and yet another "yet".
[Aside] And yet you will; and there's another "yet".
What means your ladyship? Do you not like it?
What does your ladyship mean? Don't you like it?
Yes, yes, the lines are very quaintly writ, / But, since unwillingly, take them again. / Nay, take them.
Yes, yes, the lines are very cleverly written, but since you wrote them unwillingly, take them back. No, take them.
Ay, ay, you writ them, sir, at my request, / But I will none of them. They are for you. / I would have had them writ more movingly.
Yes, yes, you wrote them, sir, because I asked you to, but I don't want them. They're for you. I would have liked them written with more feeling.
Please you, I'll write your ladyship another.
If you like, I'll write your ladyship another.
And when it's writ, for my sake read it over, / And if it please you, so; if not, why, so.
And when it's written, read it through for my sake. If you like it, good; if not, well, never mind.
If it please me, madam? What then?
If I like it, madam? What then?
Why, if it please you, take it for your labour. / And so good morrow, servant.
Why, if you like it, keep it as payment for your trouble. And so good morning, servant.

[Aside] O jest unseen, inscrutable, invisible, / As a nose on a man's face, or a weathercock on a steeple! / My master sues to her, and she hath taught her suitor, / He being her pupil, to become her tutor. / O excellent device! Was there ever heard a better? / That my master, being scribe, to himself should write the letter?

[Aside] Oh, what a joke, hidden, mysterious, invisible, as plain as the nose on a man's face or a weathervane on a steeple! My master is wooing her, and she has taught her suitor, her own pupil, to become her teacher. Oh, what a brilliant trick! Was there ever a better one? My master is the secretary, and he has to write the letter to himself!
How now, sir? What are you reasoning with yourself?
What's this, sir? What are you arguing about with yourself?
Nay, I was rhyming. 'Tis you that have the reason.
No, I was rhyming. It's you who have the reason.
To be a spokesman from Madam Silvia.
To yourself. Why, she woos you by a figure.
To yourself. Why, she's wooing you in a roundabout way.
By a letter, I should say.
Why, she hath not writ to me.
But she hasn't written to me.
What need she, when she hath made you write to yourself? Why, do you / not perceive the jest?
Why should she, when she's made you write to yourself? Why, don't you see the joke?
No believing you indeed, sir. But did you perceive her earnest?
There's no believing you, sir. But did you see she was in earnest?
She gave me none, except an angry word.
She gave me nothing but an angry word.
Why, she hath given you a letter.
Why, she's given you a letter.
That's the letter I writ to her friend.
That's the letter I wrote to her friend.
And that letter hath she delivered, and there an end.
And she's delivered that letter, and that's that.
I would it were no worse.
I wish that was all it meant.

I'll warrant you, 'tis as well. / For often have you writ to her, and she, in modesty / Or else for want of idle time, could not again reply, / Or fearing else some messenger that might her mind discover, / Herself hath taught her love himself to write unto her lover. / All this I speak in print, for in print I found it. Why muse you, sir? / 'Tis dinner time.

I promise you, it's as good as that. Because you've often written to her, and she, out of modesty or for lack of spare time, couldn't reply; or else, afraid that a messenger might give away her feelings, she has taught her lover to write to her lover himself. I'm telling you this word for word, as if I'd read it in a book. Why are you brooding, sir? It's dinner time.
Ay, but hearken, sir, though the chameleon Love can feed on the air, I / am one that am nourished by my victuals, and would fain have meat. O, / be not like your mistress! Be moved, be moved.
Yes, but listen, sir. Love may be like the chameleon and live on air, but I'm someone who's fed by food, and I'd like my dinner. Oh, don't be like your mistress! Be moved, be moved.
I must, where is no remedy.
I have to be, when nothing can be done.
When possibly I can, I will return.
I'll come back as soon as I possibly can.
If you turn not, you will return the sooner. / Keep this remembrance for thy Julia's sake.
If you don't change, you'll come back sooner. Keep this as a reminder of your Julia.
Why, then we'll make exchange. Here, take you this.
Why, then let's exchange. Here, you take this.
And seal the bargain with a holy kiss.
And seal the bargain with a holy kiss.

Here is my hand for my true constancy. / And when that hour o'erslips me in the day / Wherein I sigh not, Julia, for thy sake, / The next ensuing hour some foul mischance / Torment me for my love's forgetfulness. / My father stays my coming; answer not. / The tide is now—nay, not thy tide of tears, / That tide will stay me longer than I should. / Julia, farewell.

Here's my hand as a pledge that I'll stay true. And if an hour of any day slips past in which I don't sigh for you, Julia, let some terrible misfortune torment me the very next hour for forgetting my love. My father is waiting for me; don't answer. The tide is turning, no, not your tide of tears; that tide would keep me here longer than I should stay. Julia, farewell.
What, gone without a word? / Ay, so true love should do. It cannot speak, / For truth hath better deeds than words to grace it.
What, gone without a word? Yes, that's what true love should do. It can't speak, because truth is better honoured by actions than by words.
Sir Proteus, you are stayed for.
Sir Proteus, they're waiting for you.
Go, I come, I come. / Alas, this parting strikes poor lovers dumb.
Go on, I'm coming, I'm coming. Oh, this parting leaves poor lovers speechless.

Nay, 'twill be this hour ere I have done weeping; all the kind of the / Lances have this very fault. I have received my proportion, like the / prodigious son, and am going with Sir Proteus to the Imperial's court. / I think Crab my dog be the sourest-natured dog that lives: my mother / weeping, my father wailing, my sister crying, our maid howling, our cat / wringing her hands, and all our house in a great perplexity, yet did / not this cruel-hearted cur shed one tear. He is a stone, a very / pebblestone, and has no more pity in him than a dog. A Jew would have / wept to have seen our parting. Why, my grandam, having no eyes, look / you, wept herself blind at my parting. Nay, I'll show you the manner of / it. This shoe is my father. No, this left shoe is my father; no, no, / this left shoe is my mother. Nay, that cannot be so neither. Yes, it is / so, it is so; it hath the worser sole. This shoe with the hole in it is / my mother, and this my father. A vengeance on 't, there 'tis. Now, sir, / this staff is my sister, for, look you, she is as white as a lily and / as small as a wand. This hat is Nan, our maid. I am the dog. No, the / dog is himself, and I am the dog. O, the dog is me, and I am myself. / Ay, so, so. Now come I to my father: "Father, your blessing." Now / should not the shoe speak a word for weeping. Now should I kiss my / father. Well, he weeps on. Now come I to my mother. O, that she could / speak now like a wood woman! Well, I kiss her. Why there 'tis; here's / my mother's breath up and down. Now come I to my sister. Mark the moan / she makes. Now the dog all this while sheds not a tear nor speaks a / word; but see how I lay the dust with my tears.

No, it'll be an hour before I've finished crying. All the Lance family have this same fault. I've had my share of the inheritance, like the prodigal son, and I'm going with Sir Proteus to the Emperor's court. I think my dog Crab is the hardest-hearted dog alive. My mother was weeping, my father wailing, my sister crying, our maid howling, our cat wringing her hands and our whole house in a terrible state, and yet this cruel-hearted mutt didn't shed one tear. He's a stone, a real pebble, and he's got no more pity in him than a dog. Even a Jew would have wept to see us part. Why, my grandmother, who's got no eyes, look, cried herself blind when I left. No, I'll show you how it went. This shoe is my father. No, this left shoe is my father; no, no, this left shoe is my mother. No, that can't be right either. Yes, it is, it is: it's got the worse sole. This shoe with the hole in it is my mother, and this one is my father. Curse it, there it is. Now, sir, this stick is my sister, because, look, she's as white as a lily and as thin as a twig. This hat is Nan, our maid. I'm the dog. No, the dog is himself, and I'm the dog. Oh, the dog is me, and I'm myself. Yes, that's it, that's it. Now I come to my father: "Father, your blessing." Now the shoe should be too choked with tears to say a word. Now I should kiss my father. Well, he keeps on weeping. Now I come to my mother. Oh, if only she could talk now like a woman out of her mind! Well, I kiss her. Why, there it is: that's my mother's breath exactly. Now I come to my sister. Listen to her moaning. And all this time the dog doesn't shed a tear or say a word; but look how I'm settling the dust with my tears.
Lance, away, away! Aboard! Thy master is shipped, and thou art to post / after with oars. What's the matter? Why weep'st thou, man? Away, ass. / You'll lose the tide if you tarry any longer.

Lance, go, go! Get on board! Your master is on the ship, and you'll have to row after him. What's the matter? Why are you crying, man? Off with you, you ass. You'll miss the tide if you wait any longer.
It is no matter if the tied were lost, for it is the unkindest tied / that ever any man tied.
It wouldn't matter if the tied one were lost, because he's the cruellest tied one that anyone ever tied.
Why, he that's tied here, Crab, my dog.
Why, the one that's tied up here: Crab, my dog.

Tut, man, I mean thou'lt lose the flood, and, in losing the flood, lose / thy voyage, and, in losing thy voyage, lose thy master, and, in losing / thy master, lose thy service, and, in losing thy service—why dost thou / stop my mouth?

Nonsense, man, I mean you'll miss the high tide, and by missing the tide, miss your voyage, and by missing your voyage, lose your master, and by losing your master, lose your job, and by losing your job— Why are you covering my mouth?
For fear thou shouldst lose thy tongue.
In case you lose your tongue.
Where should I lose my tongue?
Where would I lose my tongue?

Lose the tide, and the voyage, and the master, and the service, and the / tied? Why, man, if the river were dry, I am able to fill it with my / tears; if the wind were down, I could drive the boat with my sighs.

Lose the tide, and the voyage, and the master, and the job, and the tied one? Why, man, if the river were dry, I could fill it with my tears; if the wind dropped, I could drive the boat with my sighs.
Come, come away, man. I was sent to call thee.
Come on, come away, man. I was sent to call you.
Sir, call me what thou dar'st.
Sir, call me whatever you dare.
Master, Sir Thurio frowns on you.
Master, Sir Thurio is frowning at you.
Yes, boy, it's because of love.
It would be a good idea to knock him down.
Seem you that you are not?
Do you seem to be what you're not?
What seem I that I am not?
What do I seem to be that I'm not?
What proof is there of the opposite?
And how quote you my folly?
And where do you see my foolishness?
I quote it in your jerkin.
I see it in your jacket.
Well, then, I'll double your folly.
Well then, I'll double your foolishness.
What, angry, Sir Thurio? Do you change colour?
What, angry, Sir Thurio? Are you changing colour?
Give him leave, madam, he is a kind of chameleon.
Let him be, madam. He's a sort of chameleon.
That hath more mind to feed on your blood than live in your air.
One that would rather feed on your blood than live on your air.
Ay, sir, and done too, for this time.
Yes, sir, and I've done, for now.
I know it well, sir. You always end ere you begin.
I know that well, sir. You always finish before you start.
A fine volley of words, gentlemen, and quickly shot off.
A fine volley of words, gentlemen, and quickly fired.
'Tis indeed, madam, we thank the giver.
It is indeed, madam, and we thank the person who supplied it.
Yourself, sweet lady, for you gave the fire. Sir Thurio borrows his wit / from your ladyship's looks, and spends what he borrows kindly in your / company.
You yourself, sweet lady, because you lit the fuse. Sir Thurio borrows his wit from your ladyship's looks and generously spends what he borrows in your company.
Sir, if you spend word for word with me, I shall make your wit / bankrupt.
Sir, if you trade word for word with me, I'll bankrupt your wit.
I know it well, sir. You have an exchequer of words and, I think, no / other treasure to give your followers, for it appears by their bare / liveries that they live by your bare words.
I know that well, sir. You've got a treasury of words and, I think, no other wealth to give your servants, because you can tell from their threadbare uniforms that they live on your empty words.
No more, gentlemen, no more. Here comes my father.
That's enough, gentlemen, that's enough. Here comes my father.
Now, daughter Silvia, you are hard beset. / Sir Valentine, your father is in good health. / What say you to a letter from your friends / Of much good news?
Now, daughter Silvia, you're under siege. Sir Valentine, your father is in good health. What would you say to a letter from your family with lots of good news?
My lord, I will be thankful / To any happy messenger from thence.
My lord, I'd be grateful to any messenger bringing good news from there.
Know ye Don Antonio, your countryman?
Do you know Don Antonio, from your home town?
Ay, my good lord, I know the gentleman / To be of worth and worthy estimation, / And not without desert so well reputed.
Yes, my good lord. I know the gentleman to be a man of worth and high standing, and he deserves his good reputation.
Ay, my good lord, a son that well deserves / The honour and regard of such a father.
Yes, my good lord, a son who well deserves the respect and love of such a father.

I knew him as myself, for from our infancy / We have conversed and spent our hours together. / And though myself have been an idle truant, / Omitting the sweet benefit of time / To clothe mine age with angel-like perfection, / Yet hath Sir Proteus, for that's his name, / Made use and fair advantage of his days: / His years but young, but his experience old; / His head unmellowed, but his judgement ripe; / And in a word, for far behind his worth / Comes all the praises that I now bestow, / He is complete in feature and in mind, / With all good grace to grace a gentleman.

I knew him like my own self, because we've talked and spent our time together since we were children. And though I've been a lazy truant, wasting the precious chance to use my time to make my older self perfect, Sir Proteus, for that's his name, has used his days well and to good advantage. He's young in years but old in experience; his head isn't yet grey, but his judgement is mature. In short, since all the praise I'm giving him falls far short of what he's worth, he's perfect in body and in mind, with every good quality that can grace a gentleman.

Beshrew me, sir, but if he make this good, / He is as worthy for an empress' love / As meet to be an emperor's counsellor. / Well, sir, this gentleman is come to me / With commendation from great potentates, / And here he means to spend his time awhile. / I think 'tis no unwelcome news to you.

Upon my word, sir, if he lives up to that, he's worthy of an empress's love and fit to advise an emperor. Well, sir, this gentleman has come to me with recommendations from great rulers, and he intends to stay here for a while. I don't think that's unwelcome news to you.
Should I have wished a thing, it had been he.
If I'd wished for anything, it would have been for him.
Welcome him then according to his worth. / Silvia, I speak to you, and you, Sir Thurio. / For Valentine, I need not cite him to it. / I will send him hither to you presently.
Then welcome him as he deserves. I'm speaking to you, Silvia, and to you, Sir Thurio. Valentine doesn't need telling. I'll send him to you straight away.
This is the gentleman I told your ladyship / Had come along with me but that his mistresss / Did hold his eyes locked in her crystal looks.
This is the gentleman I told your ladyship about, who would have come with me except that his mistress kept his eyes locked in her crystal gaze.
Belike that now she hath enfranchised them / Upon some other pawn for fealty.
I suppose she has freed them now, in return for some other pledge of loyalty.
Nay, sure, I think she holds them prisoners still.
No, I'm sure she still holds them prisoner.
Nay, then, he should be blind, and being blind / How could he see his way to seek out you?
No? Then he must be blind, and if he's blind, how could he see his way to come and find you?
Why, lady, Love hath twenty pair of eyes.
Why, lady, Love has twenty pairs of eyes.
They say that Love hath not an eye at all.
People say Love has no eyes at all.
To see such lovers, Thurio, as yourself. / Upon a homely object, Love can wink.
To see lovers like you, Thurio. When it comes to an ugly thing, Love can shut its eyes.
Have done, have done. Here comes the gentleman.
Stop, stop. Here comes the gentleman.
Welcome, dear Proteus! Mistress, I beseech you / Confirm his welcome with some special favour.
Welcome, dear Proteus! Mistress, please, confirm his welcome with some special favour.
His worth is warrant for his welcome hither, / If this be he you oft have wished to hear from.
His worth guarantees him a welcome here, if this is the man you've often wished to hear from.
Mistress, it is. Sweet lady, entertain him / To be my fellow-servant to your ladyship.
Mistress, it is. Sweet lady, take him on as my fellow servant to your ladyship.
Too low a mistress for so high a servant.
Too humble a mistress for so fine a servant.
Not so, sweet lady, but too mean a servant / To have a look of such a worthy mistress.
Not so, sweet lady; too lowly a servant to be looked at by such a worthy mistress.
Leave off discourse of disability. / Sweet lady, entertain him for your servant.
Stop talking about how unworthy you are. Sweet lady, take him on as your servant.
My duty will I boast of, nothing else.
I'll boast of my duty to you, and nothing else.
And duty never yet did want his meed. / Servant, you are welcome to a worthless mistress.
And duty has never gone without its reward. Servant, you're welcome to a worthless mistress.
I'll die on him that says so but yourself.
I'd fight to the death anyone but you who said that.
Madam, my lord your father would speak with you.
Madam, my lord your father wants to speak with you.
Come, Sir Thurio, / Go with me.—Once more, new servant, welcome. / I'll leave you to confer of home affairs; / When you have done, we look to hear from you.
Come, Sir Thurio, come with me. Once more, new servant, welcome. I'll leave you to talk about news from home. When you've finished, we expect to see you.
We'll both attend upon your ladyship.
We'll both come and wait on your ladyship.
Now, tell me, how do all from whence you came?
Now tell me, how is everyone back home?
Your friends are well and have them much commended.
Your family are well and send you their warm regards.
I left them all in health.
I left them all in good health.
How does your lady? And how thrives your love?
How's your lady? And how's your love going?
My tales of love were wont to weary you; / I know you joy not in a love-discourse.
My love stories used to bore you. I know you don't enjoy talk about love.

Ay, Proteus, but that life is altered now. / I have done penance for contemning Love, / Whose high imperious thoughts have punished me / With bitter fasts, with penitential groans, / With nightly tears, and daily heart-sore sighs; / For in revenge of my contempt of love, / Love hath chased sleep from my enthralled eyes / And made them watchers of mine own heart's sorrow. / O gentle Proteus, Love's a mighty lord, / And hath so humbled me as I confess / There is no woe to his correction, / Nor to his service no such joy on earth. / Now, no discourse, except it be of love; / Now can I break my fast, dine, sup, and sleep / Upon the very naked name of love.

Yes, Proteus, but my life has changed now. I've been punished for despising Love. His proud, commanding mind has made me suffer bitter fasting, groans of repentance, tears at night and heartsick sighs by day. To pay me back for scorning love, Love has driven sleep from my captive eyes and made them stay awake to watch my own heart's sorrow. Oh, gentle Proteus, Love is a mighty lord, and he's humbled me so much that I admit there's no pain like his punishment, and no joy on earth like serving him. Now I want no conversation except about love. Now I can eat breakfast, dinner and supper, and sleep, on nothing but the bare word "love".
Enough; I read your fortune in your eye. / Was this the idol that you worship so?
Enough. I can read your fortune in your eyes. Was that the idol you worship so much?
Even she; and is she not a heavenly saint?
That's her. Isn't she a heavenly saint?
No, but she is an earthly paragon.
No, but she's an earthly model of perfection.
O, flatter me, for love delights in praises.
Oh, flatter me, then, because love delights in praise.
When I was sick, you gave me bitter pills, / And I must minister the like to you.
When I was lovesick, you gave me bitter medicine, and I must give you the same.
Then speak the truth by her; if not divine, / Yet let her be a principality, / Sovereign to all the creatures on the earth.
Then tell the truth about her. If she's not divine, let her at least be an angel, ruling over every creature on earth.
Sweet, except not any, / Except thou wilt except against my love.
My dear friend, except no one, unless you mean to insult my love.
Have I not reason to prefer mine own?
Haven't I got reason to prefer my own?

And I will help thee to prefer her too: / She shall be dignified with this high honour, / To bear my lady's train, lest the base earth / Should from her vesture chance to steal a kiss, / And, of so great a favour growing proud, / Disdain to root the summer-swelling flower / And make rough winter everlastingly.

And I'll help you to promote her too: she'll be given the high honour of carrying my lady's train, in case the lowly earth steals a kiss from her dress and, grown proud of such a great favour, refuses to feed the roots of summer flowers and makes rough winter last for ever.
Why, Valentine, what braggartism is this?
Why, Valentine, what bragging is this?
Pardon me, Proteus, all I can is nothing / To her, whose worth makes other worthies nothing; / She is alone.
Forgive me, Proteus. Everything I can say is nothing compared to her, whose worth makes every other worthy person nothing. She's unique.

Not for the world! Why, man, she is mine own, / And I as rich in having such a jewel / As twenty seas, if all their sand were pearl, / The water nectar, and the rocks pure gold. / Forgive me that I do not dream on thee, / Because thou seest me dote upon my love. / My foolish rival, that her father likes / Only for his possessions are so huge, / Is gone with her along, and I must after, / For love, thou know'st, is full of jealousy.

Not for the world! Why, man, she's mine, and I'm as rich in having such a jewel as twenty seas would be if all their sand were pearls, their water nectar and their rocks pure gold. Forgive me for not thinking about you, because you can see I'm infatuated with my love. My foolish rival, whom her father likes only because his estates are so huge, has gone with her, and I must follow, because love, as you know, is full of jealousy.

Ay, and we are betrothed; nay more, our marriage hour, / With all the cunning manner of our flight, / Determined of: how I must climb her window, / The ladder made of cords, and all the means / Plotted and 'greed on for my happiness. / Good Proteus, go with me to my chamber, / In these affairs to aid me with thy counsel.

Yes, and we're engaged. More than that, we've settled the hour of our marriage and the clever way we'll run away: how I'll climb up to her window by a ladder made of ropes, and every step of the plan for my happiness is plotted and agreed. Good Proteus, come with me to my room and help me with your advice.
Go on before; I shall enquire you forth. / I must unto the road to disembark / Some necessaries that I needs must use, / And then I'll presently attend you.
You go ahead; I'll find you. I must go down to the harbour to unload some things I need, and then I'll come straight to you.

Even as one heat another heat expels, / Or as one nail by strength drives out another, / So the remembrance of my former love / Is by a newer object quite forgotten. / Is it mine eye, or Valentine's praise, / Her true perfection, or my false transgression, / That makes me reasonless to reason thus? / She is fair; and so is Julia that I love— / That I did love, for now my love is thawed, / Which like a waxen image 'gainst a fire / Bears no impression of the thing it was. / Methinks my zeal to Valentine is cold, / And that I love him not as I was wont. / O, but I love his lady too too much, / And that's the reason I love him so little. / How shall I dote on her with more advice / That thus without advice begin to love her? / 'Tis but her picture I have yet beheld, / And that hath dazzled my reason's light; / But when I look on her perfections, / There is no reason but I shall be blind. / If I can check my erring love, I will; / If not, to compass her I'll use my skill.

Just as one heat drives out another, or as one nail is forced out by another, so the memory of my old love has been completely forgotten for a newer one. Is it my eyes, or Valentine's praise, her real perfection or my false wrongdoing, that makes me reason so unreasonably? She's beautiful; and so is Julia, whom I love— whom I did love, because now my love has melted, and like a wax figure in front of a fire it keeps no trace of what it was. I think my devotion to Valentine has cooled, and I don't love him as I used to. Oh, but I love his lady far too much, and that's why I love him so little. How much more will I dote on her when I've thought it over, if I begin to love her like this without thinking? I've only seen her outward appearance so far, and that's dazzled the light of my reason; but when I see her inner perfections, I'll certainly be blinded. If I can stop my straying love, I will; if not, I'll use all my skill to win her.
Lance, by mine honesty, welcome to Milan!
Lance, on my honour, welcome to Milan!

Forswear not thyself, sweet youth, for I am not welcome. I reckon this / always, that a man is never undone till he be hanged, nor never welcome / to a place till some certain shot be paid and the hostess say / "Welcome".
Don't perjure yourself, sweet boy, because I'm not welcome. I always reckon a man is never ruined until he's hanged, and never welcome anywhere until the bill is paid and the landlady says "Welcome".
Come on, you madcap. I'll to the alehouse with you presently, where, / for one shot of five pence, thou shalt have five thousand welcomes. / But, sirrah, how did thy master part with Madam Julia?
Come on, you madman. I'll go to the pub with you right now, where for one round costing five pence you'll get five thousand welcomes. But tell me, how did your master part from Madam Julia?
Marry, after they closed in earnest, they parted very fairly in jest.
Well, after they'd embraced in earnest, they parted very nicely in jest.
How then? Shall he marry her?
What then? Will he marry her?
What, have they broken it off?
No, they are both as whole as a fish.
No, they're both as whole as a fish.
Why then, how stands the matter with them?
Well then, how do things stand between them?
Marry, thus: when it stands well with him, it stands well with her.
Well, like this: when things stand well with him, they stand well with her.
What an ass art thou! I understand thee not.
What an ass you are! I don't understand you.
What a block art thou that thou canst not! My staff understands me.
What a blockhead you are, that you can't! My stick understands me.
Ay, and what I do too. Look thee, I'll but lean, and my staff / understands me.
Yes, and what I do too. Look, I'll just lean on it, and my stick stands under me.
It does stand under you, that's true.
Why, stand-under and under-stand is all one.
Why, standing under and understanding are the same thing.
But tell me true, will't be a match?
But tell me honestly, will it be a marriage?
Ask my dog. If he say "Ay", it will; if he say "No", it will; if he / shake his tail and say nothing, it will.
Ask my dog. If he says "Yes", it will; if he says "No", it will; if he wags his tail and says nothing, it will.
The conclusion is, then, that it will.
So the answer is that it will.
Thou shalt never get such a secret from me but by a parable.
You'll never get a secret like that out of me except in a riddle.
'Tis well that I get it so. But, Lance, how sayst thou that my master / is become a notable lover?
Fine, I'll take it that way. But Lance, what do you say to my master becoming a famous lover?
I never knew him to be anything else.
A notable lubber, as thou reportest him to be.
A famous lubber, a big lump, as you say he is.
Why, thou whoreson ass, thou mistak'st me.
Why, you son-of-a-whore ass, you've got me wrong.
Why, fool, I meant not thee, I meant thy master.
Why, you fool, I didn't mean you, I meant your master.
I tell thee, my master is become a hot lover.
I'm telling you, my master has become a passionate lover.
Why, I tell thee, I care not though he burn himself in love. If thou / wilt, go with me to the alehouse; if not, thou art an Hebrew, a Jew, / and not worth the name of a Christian.
Well, I'm telling you, I don't care if he burns himself up with love. If you like, come with me to the pub; if not, you're a Hebrew, a Jew, and not worth the name of a Christian.
Because thou hast not so much charity in thee as to go to the ale with / a Christian. Wilt thou go?
Because you haven't got enough Christian charity in you to go for a drink with a fellow Christian. Will you come?

To leave my Julia, shall I be forsworn; / To love fair Silvia, shall I be forsworn; / To wrong my friend, I shall be much forsworn. / And e'en that power which gave me first my oath / Provokes me to this threefold perjury. / Love bade me swear, and Love bids me forswear. / O sweet-suggesting Love, if thou hast sinned, / Teach me, thy tempted subject, to excuse it. / At first I did adore a twinkling star, / But now I worship a celestial sun. / Unheedful vows may heedfully be broken, / And he wants wit that wants resolved will / To learn his wit t' exchange the bad for better. / Fie, fie, unreverend tongue, to call her bad / Whose sovereignty so oft thou hast preferred / With twenty thousand soul-confirming oaths. / I cannot leave to love, and yet I do; / But there I leave to love where I should love. / Julia I lose, and Valentine I lose; / If I keep them, I needs must lose myself; / If I lose them, thus find I by their loss, / For Valentine, myself; for Julia, Silvia. / I to myself am dearer than a friend, / For love is still most precious in itself, / And Silvia—witness heaven that made her fair— / Shows Julia but a swarthy Ethiope. / I will forget that Julia is alive, / Remembering that my love to her is dead; / And Valentine I'll hold an enemy, / Aiming at Silvia as a sweeter friend. / I cannot now prove constant to myself / Without some treachery used to Valentine. / This night he meaneth with a corded ladder / To climb celestial Silvia's chamber window, / Myself in counsel, his competitor. / Now presently I'll give her father notice / Of their disguising and pretended flight, / Who, all enraged, will banish Valentine, / For Thurio he intends shall wed his daughter. / But Valentine being gone, I'll quickly cross / By some sly trick blunt Thurio's dull proceeding. / Love, lend me wings to make my purpose swift, / As thou hast lent me wit to plot this drift.

If I leave my Julia, I'll break my vow; if I love beautiful Silvia, I'll break my vow; if I wrong my friend, I'll break my vow worst of all. And the very same power that made me swear in the first place drives me to break three oaths at once. Love told me to swear, and Love tells me to break my word. Oh, sweetly tempting Love, if you've sinned, teach me, your tempted subject, how to excuse it. At first I adored a twinkling star, but now I worship a heavenly sun. Thoughtless vows may be broken thoughtfully, and a man lacks sense if he lacks the willpower to teach his mind to swap bad for better. Shame, shame, irreverent tongue, to call her bad, when you've so often declared she ruled over all, with twenty thousand oaths sworn on your soul. I can't stop loving, and yet I do; but I stop loving where I should love. I lose Julia, and I lose Valentine. If I keep them, I'll have to lose myself. If I lose them, then by losing them I find myself in place of Valentine, and Silvia in place of Julia. I'm dearer to myself than any friend, because love always values itself most; and Silvia, as heaven that made her beautiful is my witness, makes Julia look like a sunburnt African. I'll forget that Julia is alive, remembering that my love for her is dead; and I'll treat Valentine as an enemy, aiming at Silvia as a sweeter friend. I can't be true to myself now without using some treachery against Valentine. Tonight he plans to climb up to heavenly Silvia's bedroom window with a rope ladder, and I, his rival, am in on the secret. I'll tell her father straight away about their disguises and planned escape. He'll be furious and banish Valentine, because he means Thurio to marry his daughter. But once Valentine is gone, I'll quickly use some sly trick to block dull Thurio's slow courtship. Love, lend me wings to make my plan move fast, as you've lent me the wit to plot it.

Counsel, Lucetta; gentle girl, assist me, / And ev'n in kind love I do conjure thee, / Who art the table wherein all my thoughts / Are visibly charactered and engraved, / To lesson me and tell me some good mean / How with my honour I may undertake / A journey to my loving Proteus.

Advise me, Lucetta; help me, gentle girl. I beg you, out of love, since you are the tablet on which all my thoughts are plainly written and engraved, teach me and tell me some good way that I can make a journey to my loving Proteus without losing my honour.
Alas, the way is wearisome and long.
Oh dear, the road is long and tiring.

A true-devoted pilgrim is not weary / To measure kingdoms with his feeble steps; / Much less shall she that hath Love's wings to fly, / And when the flight is made to one so dear, / Of such divine perfection, as Sir Proteus.

A truly devoted pilgrim isn't tired by crossing kingdoms on foot; still less will someone be who has Love's wings to fly with, especially when she's flying to someone as dear and as divinely perfect as Sir Proteus.
Better forbear till Proteus make return.
Better wait till Proteus comes back.

O, know'st thou not his looks are my soul's food? / Pity the dearth that I have pined in / By longing for that food so long a time. / Didst thou but know the inly touch of love / Thou wouldst as soon go kindle fire with snow / As seek to quench the fire of love with words.

Oh, don't you know his looks are food for my soul? Pity the famine I've been wasting away in, longing for that food for so long. If you only knew how love feels inside, you'd as soon try to light a fire with snow as try to put out the fire of love with words.
I do not seek to quench your love's hot fire, / But qualify the fire's extreme rage, / Lest it should burn above the bounds of reason.
I'm not trying to put out the hot fire of your love, only to calm its wild rage, in case it burns past the limits of reason.

The more thou damm'st it up, the more it burns. / The current that with gentle murmur glides, / Thou know'st, being stopped, impatiently doth rage; / But when his fair course is not hindered, / He makes sweet music with th' enamelled stones, / Giving a gentle kiss to every sedge / He overtaketh in his pilgrimage; / And so by many winding nooks he strays / With willing sport to the wild ocean. / Then let me go and hinder not my course. / I'll be as patient as a gentle stream / And make a pastime of each weary step / Till the last step have brought me to my love, / And there I'll rest as after much turmoil / A blessed soul doth in Elysium.

The more you dam it up, the more it burns. You know that a stream that glides along with a gentle murmur rages impatiently when it's blocked; but when its smooth course isn't held back, it makes sweet music over the shining pebbles and gives a gentle kiss to every reed it passes on its pilgrimage. And so it wanders through many winding bends, playing happily, to the wild ocean. So let me go, and don't block my course. I'll be as patient as a gentle stream and make a game of every tiring step, until the last step brings me to my love. And there I'll rest, as a blessed soul rests in heaven after much trouble.
But in what habit will you go along?
But what clothes will you wear for the journey?
Not like a woman, for I would prevent / The loose encounters of lascivious men. / Gentle Lucetta, fit me with such weeds / As may beseem some well-reputed page.
Not a woman's, because I want to avoid being pestered by lustful men. Gentle Lucetta, get me the kind of clothes a respectable page would wear.
Why then, your ladyship must cut your hair.
Why then, your ladyship will have to cut your hair.
No, girl, I'll knit it up in silken strings / With twenty odd-conceited true-love knots. / To be fantastic may become a youth / Of greater time than I shall show to be.
No, girl, I'll tie it up with silk ribbons in twenty fancy love knots. Looking showy can suit a young man even older than I'll appear to be.
What fashion, madam, shall I make your breeches?
What style shall I make your breeches, madam?
That fits as well as "Tell me, good my lord, / What compass will you wear your farthingale?" / Why e'en what fashion thou best likes, Lucetta.
That's as sensible as saying, "Tell me, my good lord, how wide will you wear your hooped skirt?" Why, whatever style you like best, Lucetta.
You must needs have them with a codpiece, madam.
You'll have to have them with a codpiece, madam.
Out, out, Lucetta, that will be ill-favoured.
Stop it, stop it, Lucetta, that would look ugly.
A round hose, madam, now's not worth a pin / Unless you have a codpiece to stick pins on.
Round breeches aren't worth a pin these days, madam, unless you've got a codpiece to stick pins in.

Lucetta, as thou lov'st me, let me have / What thou think'st meet and is most mannerly. / But tell me, wench, how will the world repute me / For undertaking so unstaid a journey? / I fear me it will make me scandalized.
Lucetta, if you love me, get me whatever you think suitable and most decent. But tell me, girl, what will people think of me for making such a reckless journey? I'm afraid it will cause a scandal.
If you think so, then stay at home and go not.
If you think so, then stay at home and don't go.
Then never dream on infamy, but go. / If Proteus like your journey when you come, / No matter who's displeased when you are gone. / I fear me he will scarce be pleased withal.

Then don't worry about your reputation, but go. If Proteus is pleased with your journey when you arrive, it doesn't matter who's displeased that you've gone. I'm afraid he won't be very pleased with it, though.
That is the least, Lucetta, of my fear. / A thousand oaths, an ocean of his tears, / And instances of infinite of love, / Warrant me welcome to my Proteus.
That's the least of my fears, Lucetta. A thousand vows, an ocean of his tears and endless proofs of his love guarantee that my Proteus will welcome me.
All these are servants to deceitful men.
Deceitful men use all those things.

Base men that use them to so base effect! / But truer stars did govern Proteus' birth. / His words are bonds, his oaths are oracles, / His love sincere, his thoughts immaculate, / His tears pure messengers sent from his heart, / His heart as far from fraud as heaven from earth.
