Low men, who use them for such low purposes! But truer stars ruled Proteus's birth. His words are binding contracts, his oaths are sacred truths, his love is sincere, his thoughts are pure, his tears are honest messengers from his heart, and his heart is as far from deceit as heaven is from earth.
Pray heav'n he prove so when you come to him.
I pray heaven he turns out like that when you get to him.

Now, as thou lov'st me, do him not that wrong / To bear a hard opinion of his truth. / Only deserve my love by loving him. / And presently go with me to my chamber / To take a note of what I stand in need of / To furnish me upon my longing journey. / All that is mine I leave at thy dispose, / My goods, my lands, my reputation; / Only, in lieu thereof, dispatch me hence. / Come, answer not, but to it presently. / I am impatient of my tarriance.

Now, if you love me, don't wrong him by thinking badly of his faithfulness. Just earn my love by loving him. Come with me to my room right now and make a list of everything I need for my longed-for journey. I leave everything I own in your hands: my goods, my lands, my good name. In return, just get me on my way. Come on, don't answer, just get to it at once. I can't bear waiting.
Sir Thurio, give us leave, I pray, awhile; / We have some secrets to confer about.
Sir Thurio, please excuse us for a while. We have some secret matters to discuss.
Now tell me, Proteus, what's your will with me?
Now tell me, Proteus, what do you want with me?

My gracious lord, that which I would discover / The law of friendship bids me to conceal, / But when I call to mind your gracious favours / Done to me, undeserving as I am, / My duty pricks me on to utter that / Which else no worldly good should draw from me. / Know, worthy prince, Sir Valentine my friend / This night intends to steal away your daughter; / Myself am one made privy to the plot. / I know you have determined to bestow her / On Thurio, whom your gentle daughter hates, / And should she thus be stol'n away from you, / It would be much vexation to your age. / Thus, for my duty's sake, I rather chose / To cross my friend in his intended drift / Than, by concealing it, heap on your head / A pack of sorrows which would press you down, / Being unprevented, to your timeless grave.

My gracious lord, the law of friendship tells me to keep secret what I'm about to reveal. But when I remember the kindness you've shown me, undeserving as I am, my duty spurs me to say what nothing in the world could otherwise drag out of me. Know, worthy prince, that my friend Sir Valentine intends to steal your daughter away tonight. I've been let in on the plot. I know you've decided to give her to Thurio, whom your gentle daughter hates, and if she were stolen away from you like this, it would be a great grief to you in your old age. So, out of duty, I chose to block my friend's plan rather than keep quiet and pile on your head a load of sorrows that, if nothing prevented them, would weigh you down into an early grave.

Proteus, I thank thee for thine honest care, / Which to requite command me while I live. / This love of theirs myself have often seen, / Haply when they have judged me fast asleep, / And oftentimes have purposed to forbid / Sir Valentine her company and my court. / But fearing lest my jealous aim might err / And so, unworthily, disgrace the man— / A rashness that I ever yet have shunned— / I gave him gentle looks, thereby to find / That which thyself hast now disclosed to me. / And that thou mayst perceive my fear of this, / Knowing that tender youth is soon suggested, / I nightly lodge her in an upper tower, / The key whereof myself have ever kept; / And thence she cannot be conveyed away.

Proteus, thank you for your honest concern. To repay it, call on me as long as I live. I've often seen this love of theirs myself, perhaps when they thought I was fast asleep, and I've often meant to ban Sir Valentine from her company and from my court. But I was afraid my suspicions might be wrong and so disgrace the man unfairly, a rash thing I've always avoided. So I was friendly to him, in order to find out what you've now told me. And so that you can see how I've feared this, knowing that young people are easily tempted, I make her sleep each night in an upper tower, and I always keep the key myself. She can't be carried off from there.

Know, noble lord, they have devised a mean / How he her chamber-window will ascend / And with a corded ladder fetch her down; / For which the youthful lover now is gone, / And this way comes he with it presently, / Where, if it please you, you may intercept him. / But, good my lord, do it so cunningly / That my discovery be not aimed at; / For love of you, not hate unto my friend, / Hath made me publisher of this pretence.

Know, noble lord, they've worked out a way for him to climb up to her bedroom window and bring her down with a rope ladder. The young lover has gone to fetch it now, and he'll come this way with it soon. Here you can stop him, if you like. But, my good lord, do it so cleverly that no one guesses I told you. It's love for you, not hatred for my friend, that has made me reveal this plan.
Upon mine honour, he shall never know / That I had any light from thee of this.
On my honour, he'll never know that you told me anything about this.
Adieu, my lord, Sir Valentine is coming.
Goodbye, my lord. Sir Valentine is coming.
Sir Valentine, whither away so fast?
Sir Valentine, where are you off to in such a hurry?
Please it your Grace, there is a messenger / That stays to bear my letters to my friends, / And I am going to deliver them.
If it please your grace, there's a messenger waiting to take my letters to my family, and I'm going to give them to him.
The tenor of them doth but signify / My health and happy being at your court.
All they say is that I'm well and happy at your court.

Nay then, no matter. Stay with me awhile; / I am to break with thee of some affairs / That touch me near, wherein thou must be secret. / 'Tis not unknown to thee that I have sought / To match my friend Sir Thurio to my daughter.

No? Then it doesn't matter. Stay with me a while. I need to talk to you about some matters that concern me closely, and you must keep them secret. You know that I've been trying to marry my friend Sir Thurio to my daughter.

I know it well, my lord, and sure the match / Were rich and honourable. Besides, the gentleman / Is full of virtue, bounty, worth, and qualities / Beseeming such a wife as your fair daughter. / Cannot your grace win her to fancy him?

I know it well, my lord, and surely the match would be rich and honourable. Besides, the gentleman is full of virtue, generosity, worth and qualities that suit a wife like your beautiful daughter. Can't your grace persuade her to like him?

No, trust me, she is peevish, sullen, froward, / Proud, disobedient, stubborn, lacking duty, / Neither regarding that she is my child / Nor fearing me as if I were her father; / And, may I say to thee, this pride of hers, / Upon advice, hath drawn my love from her, / And where I thought the remnant of mine age / Should have been cherished by her childlike duty, / I now am full resolved to take a wife / And turn her out to who will take her in. / Then let her beauty be her wedding dower, / For me and my possessions she esteems not.

No, believe me, she's sulky, moody, contrary, proud, disobedient, stubborn and undutiful. She cares nothing that she's my child, and she isn't afraid of me as she should be of her father. And, I can tell you, this pride of hers, after some thought, has turned my love away from her. I thought the rest of my old age would be cared for by her duty as a daughter, but now I've firmly decided to take a wife and throw her out to whoever will take her in. Then let her beauty be her dowry, since she cares nothing for me or my wealth.
What would your Grace have me to do in this?
What would your grace like me to do about this?

There is a lady of Verona here / Whom I affect; but she is nice, and coy, / And nought esteems my aged eloquence. / Now therefore would I have thee to my tutor— / For long agone I have forgot to court; / Besides, the fashion of the time is changed— / How and which way I may bestow myself / To be regarded in her sun-bright eye.

There's a lady here from Verona whom I'm fond of, but she's fussy and shy, and thinks nothing of an old man's fine speeches. So I'd like you to be my teacher, because I forgot how to court long ago, and besides, fashions have changed. Teach me how to behave so that her sun-bright eyes will notice me.
Win her with gifts if she respect not words; / Dumb jewels often in their silent kind / More than quick words do move a woman's mind.
Win her with presents if she doesn't care for words. Silent jewels, quiet as they are, often move a woman's heart more than lively words.
But she did scorn a present that I sent her.
But she rejected a present I sent her.

A woman sometime scorns what best contents her. / Send her another; never give her o'er, / For scorn at first makes after-love the more. / If she do frown, 'tis not in hate of you, / But rather to beget more love in you. / If she do chide, 'tis not to have you gone, / Forwhy the fools are mad if left alone. / Take no repulse, whatever she doth say; / For "Get you gone" she doth not mean "Away!" / Flatter and praise, commend, extol their graces; / Though ne'er so black, say they have angels' faces. / That man that hath a tongue, I say, is no man / If with his tongue he cannot win a woman.

A woman sometimes rejects what pleases her most. Send her another; never give up on her, because scorn at first makes love stronger later. If she frowns, it isn't because she hates you, but to make you love her more. If she scolds you, it isn't because she wants you gone, because the silly things go mad if they're left alone. Don't be put off, whatever she says, because when she says "Get out" she doesn't mean "Go away!" Flatter and praise them, admire and extol their charms; however dark-skinned they are, say they have angels' faces. I say the man who has a tongue is no man if he can't win a woman with it.
But she I mean is promised by her friends / Unto a youthful gentleman of worth, / And kept severely from resort of men, / That no man hath access by day to her.
But the lady I mean has been promised by her family to a fine young gentleman, and she's kept strictly away from men, so no man can see her by day.
Why then, I would resort to her by night.
Why then, I'd visit her by night.
Ay, but the doors be locked and keys kept safe, / That no man hath recourse to her by night.
Yes, but the doors are locked and the keys kept safe, so no man can get to her by night.
What lets but one may enter at her window?
What's to stop someone climbing in at her window?
Her chamber is aloft, far from the ground, / And built so shelving that one cannot climb it / Without apparent hazard of his life.
Her room is high up, far from the ground, and the wall leans out so far that no one could climb it without obviously risking his life.
Why, then a ladder quaintly made of cords / To cast up with a pair of anchoring hooks, / Would serve to scale another Hero's tower, / So bold Leander would adventure it.
Why, then a cleverly made rope ladder, thrown up with a pair of grappling hooks, would do to climb another Hero's tower, if a bold Leander would risk it.
Now, as thou art a gentleman of blood, / Advise me where I may have such a ladder.
Now, as you're a well-born gentleman, tell me where I can get a ladder like that.
When would you use it? Pray, sir, tell me that.
When would you use it? Please, sir, tell me that.
This very night; for Love is like a child / That longs for everything that he can come by.
This very night; because Love is like a child, wanting everything it can get hold of.
By seven o'clock I'll get you such a ladder.
I'll get you a ladder like that by seven o'clock.
But, hark thee: I will go to her alone; / How shall I best convey the ladder thither?
But listen: I'll go to her alone. How can I best carry the ladder there?
It will be light, my lord, that you may bear it / Under a cloak that is of any length.
It'll be light, my lord, so you can carry it under any reasonably long cloak.
A cloak as long as thine will serve the turn?
Would a cloak as long as yours do?
Then let me see thy cloak; / I'll get me one of such another length.
Then let me see your cloak. I'll get myself one of the same length.
Why, any cloak will serve the turn, my lord.
Why, any cloak will do, my lord.
How shall I fashion me to wear a cloak? / I pray thee, let me feel thy cloak upon me.
How do I wear a cloak like this? Please, let me try your cloak on.
What letter is this same? What's here?—To Silvia? / And here an engine fit for my proceeding. / I'll be so bold to break the seal for once.
What's this letter? What's this? "To Silvia"? And here's just the tool for my purpose. I'll be so bold as to break the seal for once.

[Reads] My thoughts do harbour with my Silvia nightly, / And slaves they are to me that send them flying. / O, could their master come and go as lightly, / Himself would lodge where, senseless, they are lying. / My herald thoughts in thy pure bosom rest them, / While I, their king, that thither them importune, / Do curse the grace that with such grace hath blest them, / Because myself do want my servants' fortune. / I curse myself, for they are sent by me, / That they should harbour where their lord should be. / What's here? / [Reads] Silvia, this night I will enfranchise thee. / 'Tis so; and here's the ladder for the purpose. / Why, Phaëthon—for thou art Merops' son— / Wilt thou aspire to guide the heavenly car, / And with thy daring folly burn the world? / Wilt thou reach stars because they shine on thee? / Go, base intruder, overweening slave, / Bestow thy fawning smiles on equal mates, / And think my patience, more than thy desert, / Is privilege for thy departure hence. / Thank me for this more than for all the favours / Which, all too much, I have bestowed on thee. / But if thou linger in my territories / Longer than swiftest expedition / Will give thee time to leave our royal court, / By heaven, my wrath shall far exceed the love / I ever bore my daughter or thyself. / Begone, I will not hear thy vain excuse, / But, as thou lov'st thy life, make speed from hence.

[Reads] "My thoughts stay with my Silvia every night, and they are slaves to me, who sends them flying to her. Oh, if their master could come and go as easily, he would lie himself where they lie, unfeeling. My messenger thoughts rest in your pure breast, while I, their king, who urges them to go there, curse the good luck that has blessed them so, because I lack my servants' fortune. I curse myself, because I send them, so that they lodge where their lord should be." What's this? [Reads] "Silvia, tonight I will set you free." So that's it; and here's the ladder for the job. Why, Phaethon, for you're a nobody like Merops's son, will you try to drive the sun's chariot and burn up the world with your reckless folly? Will you reach for the stars just because they shine on you? Go, low intruder, presumptuous slave! Give your fawning smiles to your equals, and think that my patience, not what you deserve, is what allows you to leave. Thank me for this more than for all the favours I've given you, far too many. But if you stay in my lands longer than the fastest journey takes to leave our royal court, by heaven, my anger will far exceed any love I ever had for my daughter or for you. Get out. I won't listen to your useless excuses. If you value your life, leave here quickly.

And why not death, rather than living torment? / To die is to be banished from myself, / And Silvia is myself; banished from her / Is self from self—a deadly banishment. / What light is light, if Silvia be not seen? / What joy is joy, if Silvia be not by? / Unless it be to think that she is by / And feed upon the shadow of perfection. / Except I be by Silvia in the night, / There is no music in the nightingale. / Unless I look on Silvia in the day, / There is no day for me to look upon. / She is my essence, and I leave to be / If I be not by her fair influence / Fostered, illumined, cherished, kept alive. / I fly not death, to fly his deadly doom: / Tarry I here, I but attend on death, / But fly I hence, I fly away from life.

And why not death, rather than this living torture? To die is to be banished from myself, and Silvia is myself. To be banished from her is to be cut off from my own self: a deadly banishment. What light is light, if I can't see Silvia? What joy is joy, if Silvia isn't near? Unless I imagine she's near and feed on the shadow of perfection. Unless I'm with Silvia at night, there's no music in the nightingale. Unless I see Silvia by day, there's no daylight for me to see. She's my very being, and I'll cease to exist if her lovely influence doesn't nourish, light, cherish and keep me alive. I don't escape death by escaping his death sentence: if I stay here, I'm only waiting for death, but if I go away from here, I'm running away from life.
Run, boy, run, run, seek him out.
Run, boy, run, run, find him.
Him we go to find. There's not a hair on 's head but 'tis a Valentine.
The man we're looking for. There's not a hair on his head that isn't a Valentine.
Can nothing speak? Master, shall I strike?
Can nothing speak? Master, shall I hit him?
Why, sir, I'll strike nothing. I pray you—
Why, sir, I'll hit nothing. Please let me—
Sirrah, I say, forbear.—Friend Valentine, a word.
I said stop it, boy. Valentine, my friend, a word.
My ears are stopped and cannot hear good news, / So much of bad already hath possessed them.
My ears are blocked and can't hear good news, they're so full of bad already.
Then in dumb silence will I bury mine, / For they are harsh, untuneable, and bad.
Then I'll bury my news in silence, because it's harsh, unpleasant and bad.
No Valentine indeed for sacred Silvia. / Hath she forsworn me?
No Valentine, indeed, for sacred Silvia. Has she rejected me?
No Valentine, if Silvia have forsworn me. / What is your news?
No Valentine, if Silvia has rejected me. What's your news?
Sir, there is a proclamation that you are vanished.
Sir, there's a proclamation that you've vanished.
That thou art banished—O, that's the news— / From hence, from Silvia, and from me thy friend.
That you're banished, oh, that's the news, from here, from Silvia and from me, your friend.
O, I have fed upon this woe already, / And now excess of it will make me surfeit. / Doth Silvia know that I am banished?
Oh, I've already fed on this sorrow, and now too much of it will make me sick. Does Silvia know I'm banished?

Ay, ay; and she hath offered to the doom— / Which unreversed stands in effectual force— / A sea of melting pearl, which some call tears; / Those at her father's churlish feet she tendered, / With them, upon her knees, her humble self, / Wringing her hands, whose whiteness so became them / As if but now they waxed pale for woe. / But neither bended knees, pure hands held up, / Sad sighs, deep groans, nor silver-shedding tears / Could penetrate her uncompassionate sire; / But Valentine, if he be ta'en, must die. / Besides, her intercession chafed him so, / When she for thy repeal was suppliant, / That to close prison he commanded her, / With many bitter threats of biding there.

Yes, yes; and she has offered up against the sentence, which still stands, a sea of melting pearls that some call tears. She poured them at her father's harsh feet, and with them, on her knees, she offered her humble self, wringing her hands, whose whiteness suited them so well it was as if they had just turned pale with grief. But neither bended knees, pure hands raised up, sad sighs, deep groans nor silver tears could move her pitiless father: if Valentine is caught, he must die. Besides, her pleading for your pardon made him so angry that he ordered her locked up, with many bitter threats that she would stay there.
No more, unless the next word that thou speak'st / Have some malignant power upon my life. / If so, I pray thee breathe it in mine ear, / As ending anthem of my endless dolour.
No more, unless the next word you say has power to kill me. If it does, please breathe it into my ear, as the last hymn of my endless sorrow.

Cease to lament for that thou canst not help, / And study help for that which thou lament'st. / Time is the nurse and breeder of all good. / Here if thou stay, thou canst not see thy love; / Besides, thy staying will abridge thy life. / Hope is a lover's staff; walk hence with that / And manage it against despairing thoughts. / Thy letters may be here, though thou art hence, / Which, being writ to me, shall be delivered / Even in the milk-white bosom of thy love. / The time now serves not to expostulate. / Come, I'll convey thee through the city-gate, / And, ere I part with thee, confer at large / Of all that may concern thy love affairs. / As thou lov'st Silvia, though not for thyself, / Regard thy danger, and along with me.

Stop grieving over what you can't help, and work out how to help what you're grieving over. Time is the nurse and parent of everything good. If you stay here, you can't see your love; besides, staying will cut your life short. Hope is a lover's walking stick: walk away from here with it and use it to fight off despairing thoughts. Your letters can be here even if you're away. If you write them to me, I'll deliver them right into your love's milk-white bosom. Now isn't the time to argue. Come, I'll take you through the city gate, and before we part we'll talk at length about everything to do with your love. If you love Silvia, even if you don't care about yourself, think of the danger and come with me.
I pray thee, Lance, an if thou seest my boy, / Bid him make haste and meet me at the North Gate.
Please, Lance, if you see my boy, tell him to hurry and meet me at the North Gate.
Go, sirrah, find him out. Come, Valentine.
Go and find him, boy. Come, Valentine.
O, my dear Silvia! Hapless Valentine!
Oh, my dear Silvia! Unlucky Valentine!

I am but a fool, look you, and yet I have the wit to think my master is / a kind of a knave; but that's all one if he be but one knave. He lives / not now that knows me to be in love, yet I am in love, but a team of / horse shall not pluck that from me, nor who 'tis I love; and yet 'tis a / woman, but what woman I will not tell myself; and yet 'tis a milkmaid; / yet 'tis not a maid, for she hath had gossips; yet 'tis a maid, for she / is her master's maid and serves for wages. She hath more qualities than / a water-spaniel, which is much in a bare Christian. [Pulls out a paper] / Here is the cate-log of her condition. Imprimis, She can / fetch and carry. Why, a horse can do no more; nay, a horse cannot / fetch but only carry; therefore is she better than a jade. Item, She / can milk. Look you, a sweet virtue in a maid with clean hands.

I'm only a fool, you see, and yet I've got the sense to think my master is a kind of knave; but that's all one, as long as he's only one knave. There's no one alive who knows I'm in love, and yet I'm in love, but a team of horses won't drag that out of me, nor who it is I love. And yet it's a woman, but which woman I won't tell even myself. And yet it's a milkmaid. And yet she's not a maid, because she's had a baby christened. And yet she is a maid, because she's her master's maid and works for wages. She has more good qualities than a water spaniel, which is a lot for a mere Christian. [Pulls out a paper] Here's the catalogue of her qualities. "First, she can fetch and carry." Why, a horse can do no more than that; no, a horse can't fetch, only carry, so she's better than a nag. "Next, she can milk." Look, that's a sweet virtue in a girl with clean hands.
How now, Signior Lance? What news with your mastership?
Hello, Signior Lance! What news with your mastership?
With my master's ship? Why, it is at sea.
With my master's ship? Why, it's at sea.
Well, your old vice still: mistake the word. What news, then, in your / paper?
Well, your old fault again: getting the word wrong. What news is in your paper, then?
The blackest news that ever thou heard'st.
The blackest news you ever heard.
Fie on thee, jolt-head, thou canst not read.
Shame on you, blockhead, you can't read.
I will try thee. Tell me this, who begot thee?
I'll test you. Tell me this: who was your father?
Marry, the son of my grandfather.
O, illiterate loiterer! It was the son of thy grandmother. / This proves that thou canst not read.
Oh, you illiterate idler! It was your grandmother's son. That proves you can't read.
Come, fool, come; try me in thy paper.
Come on, fool, come on; test me with your paper.
[Gives him the paper] There; and Saint Nicholas be thy speed.
[Gives him the paper] There, and Saint Nicholas, the patron of scholars, help you.
And thereof comes the proverb, "Blessing of your heart, you brew good / ale."
And that's where the saying comes from: "Bless your heart, you brew good ale."
That's as much as to say, "Can she so?"
That's as good as asking, "Can she, so?"
What need a man care for a stock with a wench, when she can knit him a / stock?
Why should a man worry about a dowry with a girl, when she can knit him stockings?
Item, She can wash and scour.
A special virtue, for then she need not be washed and scoured.
A special virtue, because then she won't need washing and scrubbing herself.
Then may I set the world on wheels, when she can spin for her living.
Then I can take life easy, since she can spin for her living.
Item, She hath many nameless virtues.
That's as much as to say, "bastard virtues", that indeed know not their / fathers, and therefore have no names.
That's as good as saying "bastard virtues", which don't know their fathers and so have no names.
Close at the heels of her virtues.
Hard on the heels of her virtues.
Item, She is not to be kissed fasting in respect of her breath.
"Next, she mustn't be kissed before breakfast, because of her breath."
Well, that fault may be mended with a breakfast. / Read on.
Well, a breakfast will fix that fault. Read on.
Item, She hath a sweet mouth.
That makes amends for her sour breath.
That makes up for her sour breath.
Item, She doth talk in her sleep.
It's no matter for that, so she sleep not in her talk.
That doesn't matter, as long as she doesn't sleep while she's talking.
Item, She is slow in words.
O villain, that set this down among her vices! To be slow in words is a / woman's only virtue. I pray thee, out with't, and place it for her / chief virtue.
Oh, what a villain to put that among her faults! Being slow to speak is a woman's only virtue. Please, take it out of there and put it down as her chief virtue.
Out with that too; it was Eve's legacy and cannot be ta'en from her.
Take that out too. It was Eve's legacy, and it can't be taken from her.
I care not for that neither, because I love crusts.
I don't mind that either, because I love crusts.
Well, the best is, she hath no teeth to bite.
Well, the good thing is, she has no teeth to bite with.
Item, She will often praise her liquor.
"Next, she will often praise her drink."
If her liquor be good, she shall; if she will not, I will, for good / things should be praised.
If her drink is good, she can; if she won't, I will, because good things should be praised.
Of her tongue she cannot, for that's writ down she is slow of; of her / purse she shall not, for that I'll keep shut. Now, of another thing she / may, and that cannot I help. Well, proceed.
Not with her tongue, because it says she's slow to speak; not with her purse, because I'll keep that shut. Now, she may be free with something else, and I can't help that. Well, go on.
Item, She hath more hair than wit, and more faults than hairs, and / more wealth than faults.
"Next, she has more hair than brains, and more faults than hairs, and more money than faults."
Stop there; I'll have her. She was mine and not mine twice or thrice in / that last article. Rehearse that once more.
Stop there, I'll have her. She was mine and not mine two or three times in that last item. Read that once more.
Item, She hath more hair than wit—
"Next, she has more hair than brains—"

More hair than wit. It may be; I'll prove it: the cover of the salt / hides the salt, and therefore it is more than the salt; the hair that / covers the wit is more than the wit, for the greater hides the less. / What's next?

More hair than brains. That may be; I'll prove it. The lid of the salt cellar hides the salt, so it's bigger than the salt; the hair that covers the brains is more than the brains, because the bigger thing hides the smaller. What's next?
That's monstrous! O, that that were out!
That's monstrous! Oh, I wish that were left out!
Why, that word makes the faults gracious. Well, I'll have her; an if it / be a match, as nothing is impossible—
Why, that word makes the faults attractive. Well, I'll have her; and if we marry, since nothing's impossible—
Why, then will I tell thee that thy master stays for thee at the North / Gate.
Why, then I'll tell you that your master is waiting for you at the North Gate.
For thee? Ay, who art thou? He hath stayed for a better man than thee.
For you? Yes, who do you think you are? He's waited for a better man than you.
And must I go to him?
And do I have to go to him?
Thou must run to him, for thou hast stayed so long that going will / scarce serve the turn.
You have to run to him, because you've stayed so long that walking won't be fast enough.
Why didst not tell me sooner? Pox of your love letters!
Why didn't you tell me sooner? Plague take your love letters!
Now will he be swinged for reading my letter; an unmannerly slave, that / will thrust himself into secrets. I'll after, to rejoice in the boy's / correction.
Now he'll be beaten for reading my letter. The rude rascal, poking his nose into secrets. I'll follow him and enjoy watching the boy get punished.
Sir Thurio, fear not but that she will love you / Now Valentine is banished from her sight.
Sir Thurio, don't worry: she'll love you now that Valentine is banished from her sight.
Since his exile she hath despised me most, / Forsworn my company and railed at me, / That I am desperate of obtaining her.
Since he was exiled she has despised me more than ever. She refuses to see me and abuses me, so I've given up hope of winning her.

This weak impress of love is as a figure / Trenched in ice, which with an hour's heat / Dissolves to water and doth lose his form. / A little time will melt her frozen thoughts, / And worthless Valentine shall be forgot.

This faint imprint of love is like a figure carved in ice, which an hour's heat melts to water so that it loses its shape. A little time will thaw her frozen thoughts, and worthless Valentine will be forgotten.
How now, Sir Proteus? Is your countryman, / According to our proclamation, gone?
Well, Sir Proteus? Has your fellow countryman gone, as our proclamation ordered?
My daughter takes his going grievously.
My daughter is taking his departure badly.
A little time, my lord, will kill that grief.
A little time will kill that grief, my lord.
So I believe, but Thurio thinks not so. / Proteus, the good conceit I hold of thee, / For thou hast shown some sign of good desert, / Makes me the better to confer with thee.
So I believe, but Thurio doesn't think so. Proteus, my good opinion of you, since you've shown signs of being trustworthy, makes me readier to consult you.
Longer than I prove loyal to your Grace / Let me not live to look upon your Grace.
If I ever stop being loyal to your grace, let me not live to see your grace again.
Thou know'st how willingly I would effect / The match between Sir Thurio and my daughter?
You know how much I want to bring about the marriage between Sir Thurio and my daughter?
And also, I think, thou art not ignorant / How she opposes her against my will?
And I think you also know how she sets herself against my wishes?
She did, my lord, when Valentine was here.
She did, my lord, while Valentine was here.
Ay, and perversely she persevers so. / What might we do to make the girl forget / The love of Valentine, and love Sir Thurio?
Yes, and she stubbornly keeps it up. What could we do to make the girl forget her love for Valentine and love Sir Thurio?
The best way is to slander Valentine / With falsehood, cowardice, and poor descent, / Three things that women highly hold in hate.
The best way is to slander Valentine, accusing him of dishonesty, cowardice and low birth, three things women hate most.
Ay, but she'll think that it is spoke in hate.
Yes, but she'll think it's said out of hatred.
Ay, if his enemy deliver it; / Therefore it must with circumstance be spoken / By one whom she esteemeth as his friend.
Yes, if his enemy says it. So it must be said, with convincing detail, by someone she thinks of as his friend.
Then you must undertake to slander him.
Then you must take on the job of slandering him.
And that, my lord, I shall be loath to do. / 'Tis an ill office for a gentleman, / Especially against his very friend.
And that, my lord, I'd be very unwilling to do. It's a nasty job for a gentleman, especially against his own close friend.
Where your good word cannot advantage him, / Your slander never can endamage him; / Therefore the office is indifferent, / Being entreated to it by your friend.
Since your good word can't help him, your slander can't hurt him. So the job is neither good nor bad, especially when your friend asks you to do it.

You have prevailed, my lord. If I can do it / By aught that I can speak in his dispraise, / She shall not long continue love to him. / But say this weed her love from Valentine, / It follows not that she will love Sir Thurio.

You've persuaded me, my lord. If anything I can say against him will do it, she won't go on loving him for long. But say this weeds her love away from Valentine, it doesn't follow that she'll love Sir Thurio.

Therefore, as you unwind her love from him, / Lest it should ravel and be good to none, / You must provide to bottom it on me, / Which must be done by praising me as much / As you in worth dispraise Sir Valentine.
So as you unwind her love from him, in case it tangles and is no good to anyone, you must make sure you wind it onto me. And that must be done by praising me as much as you run down Sir Valentine.

And, Proteus, we dare trust you in this kind / Because we know, on Valentine's report, / You are already Love's firm votary / And cannot soon revolt and change your mind. / Upon this warrant shall you have access / Where you with Silvia may confer at large— / For she is lumpish, heavy, melancholy, / And, for your friend's sake, will be glad of you— / Where you may temper her by your persuasion / To hate young Valentine and love my friend.

And, Proteus, we can trust you in this, because we know from Valentine that you're already a faithful servant of Love and won't quickly turn and change your mind. On that guarantee, you'll be allowed in to see Silvia and talk with her as much as you like. She's dull, heavy and melancholy, and for your friend's sake she'll be glad of your company. There you can use your powers of persuasion to soften her into hating young Valentine and loving my friend.

As much as I can do I will effect. / But you, Sir Thurio, are not sharp enough. / You must lay lime to tangle her desires / By wailful sonnets, whose composed rhymes / Should be full-fraught with serviceable vows.
I'll do as much as I can. But you, Sir Thurio, aren't eager enough. You must set traps to catch her desires, with mournful sonnets whose carefully made rhymes are packed with promises of service.
Ay, much is the force of heaven-bred poesy.
Yes, heaven-sent poetry has great power.

Say that upon the altar of her beauty / You sacrifice your tears, your sighs, your heart. / Write till your ink be dry, and with your tears / Moist it again, and frame some feeling line / That may discover such integrity. / For Orpheus' lute was strung with poets' sinews, / Whose golden touch could soften steel and stones, / Make tigers tame, and huge leviathans / Forsake unsounded deeps to dance on sands. / After your dire-lamenting elegies, / Visit by night your lady's chamber-window / With some sweet consort; to their instruments / Tune a deploring dump; the night's dead silence / Will well become such sweet-complaining grievance. / This, or else nothing, will inherit her.

Tell her that on the altar of her beauty you sacrifice your tears, your sighs, your heart. Write till your ink runs dry, then wet it again with your tears, and make up some moving line that shows how true you are. Because Orpheus's lute was strung with poets' heartstrings, and its golden touch could soften steel and stones, tame tigers and make huge sea monsters leave the bottomless deep to dance on the sand. After your sad, lamenting love poems, go by night to your lady's bedroom window with a group of sweet musicians. Have them play a mournful tune; the dead silence of the night will suit such sweet complaints of grief. This will win her, or nothing will.
This discipline shows thou hast been in love.
Your lessons show you've been in love.

And thy advice this night I'll put in practice. / Therefore, sweet Proteus, my direction-giver, / Let us into the city presently / To sort some gentlemen well skilled in music. / I have a sonnet that will serve the turn / To give the onset to thy good advice.

And I'll put your advice into practice tonight. So, sweet Proteus, my instructor, let's go into the city now to pick out some gentlemen who are good at music. I've got a sonnet that will do to make a start on your good advice.
We'll wait upon your Grace till after supper, / And afterward determine our proceedings.
We'll attend your grace till after supper, and then decide what to do.
Even now about it! I will pardon you.
Get on with it right now! I excuse you.
Fellows, stand fast. I see a passenger.
Hold your ground, lads. I can see a traveller.
If there be ten, shrink not, but down with 'em.
If there are ten of them, don't back off. Knock them down.
Stand, sir, and throw us that you have about ye. / If not, we'll make you sit, and rifle you.
Stop, sir, and throw down whatever you've got on you. If not, we'll make you sit and search you.
Sir, we are undone: these are the villains / That all the travellers do fear so much.
Sir, we're done for. These are the villains every traveller is so afraid of.
That's not so, sir. We are your enemies.
That's not so, sir. We're your enemies.
Ay, by my beard, will we, for he is a proper man.
Yes, by my beard, we will, because he's a fine-looking man.

Then know that I have little wealth to lose. / A man I am crossed with adversity; / My riches are these poor habiliments, / Of which if you should here disfurnish me, / You take the sum and substance that I have.
Then know that I have little money to lose. I'm a man dogged by bad luck. My only wealth is these poor clothes, and if you strip me of them, you take everything I own.
Some sixteen months, and longer might have stayed / If crooked fortune had not thwarted me.
About sixteen months, and I might have stayed longer if crooked fortune hadn't thwarted me.
What, were you banished from there?
For that which now torments me to rehearse; / I killed a man, whose death I much repent, / But yet I slew him manfully in fight, / Without false vantage or base treachery.
For something it torments me to talk about. I killed a man, and I deeply regret his death; but I killed him bravely in a fair fight, without taking unfair advantage or using low tricks.
Why, ne'er repent it, if it were done so. / But were you banished for so small a fault?
Why, never regret it, if it was done like that. But were you banished for such a small offence?
I was, and held me glad of such a doom.
I was, and I was glad to get such a light sentence.
My youthful travel therein made me happy, / Or else I often had been miserable.
My travels as a young man gave me that skill, or I would often have been in trouble.
By the bare scalp of Robin Hood's fat friar, / This fellow were a king for our wild faction.
By the bald head of Robin Hood's fat friar, this fellow would make a king for our wild gang.
We'll have him. Sirs, a word.
We'll have him. Lads, a word.
Master, be one of them. It's an honourable kind of thievery.
Master, join them. It's an honourable kind of thieving.
Tell us this: have you anything to take to?
Tell us this: have you anything to live on?

Know then that some of us are gentlemen, / Such as the fury of ungoverned youth / Thrust from the company of awful men. / Myself was from Verona banished / For practising to steal away a lady, / An heir, and near allied unto the Duke.

Then know that some of us are gentlemen, driven out of respectable society by the wildness of our unruly youth. I was banished from Verona for trying to run off with a lady, an heiress and a close relative of the Duke.
And I from Mantua, for a gentleman / Who, in my mood, I stabbed unto the heart.
And I from Mantua, for a gentleman I stabbed to the heart in a fit of temper.

And I for suchlike petty crimes as these. / But to the purpose, for we cite our faults, / That they may hold excused our lawless lives; / And partly, seeing you are beautified / With goodly shape, and by your own report / A linguist, and a man of such perfection / As we do in our quality much want—

And I for petty crimes like these. But to the point. We tell you our crimes to excuse our lawless lives. And partly because we see you're blessed with good looks and, by your own account, can speak languages, and are the sort of accomplished man our trade badly needs—
Indeed because you are a banished man, / Therefore, above the rest, we parley to you. / Are you content to be our general? / To make a virtue of necessity / And live as we do in this wilderness?
To be honest, because you're a banished man, we're making you this offer above anyone else. Will you agree to be our leader, make a virtue of necessity and live as we do in this wilderness?
What sayst thou? Wilt thou be of our consort? / Say "Ay", and be the captain of us all, / We'll do thee homage and be ruled by thee, / Love thee as our commander and our king.
What do you say? Will you join our band? Say "Yes" and be captain of us all. We'll swear loyalty to you and be ruled by you, and love you as our commander and our king.
But if thou scorn our courtesy, thou diest.
But if you scorn our kind offer, you die.
Thou shalt not live to brag what we have offered.
You won't live to boast about what we offered you.
I take your offer and will live with you, / Provided that you do no outrages / On silly women or poor passengers.
I accept your offer and will live with you, provided you don't commit any outrages against defenceless women or poor travellers.
No, we detest such vile base practices. / Come, go with us; we'll bring thee to our crews / And show thee all the treasure we have got, / Which, with ourselves, all rest at thy dispose.
No, we hate such vile, low behaviour. Come with us. We'll take you to the rest of our men and show you all the treasure we've got, which, along with ourselves, is all at your command.

Already have I been false to Valentine, / And now I must be as unjust to Thurio. / Under the colour of commending him, / I have access my own love to prefer. / But Silvia is too fair, too true, too holy / To be corrupted with my worthless gifts. / When I protest true loyalty to her, / She twits me with my falsehood to my friend; / When to her beauty I commend my vows, / She bids me think how I have been forsworn / In breaking faith with Julia, whom I loved; / And notwithstanding all her sudden quips, / The least whereof would quell a lover's hope, / Yet, spaniel-like, the more she spurns my love, / The more it grows and fawneth on her still. / But here comes Thurio. Now must we to her window, / And give some evening music to her ear.

I've already been false to Valentine, and now I must be just as unfair to Thurio. Pretending to speak up for him, I get the chance to push my own love. But Silvia is too beautiful, too faithful, too holy to be corrupted by my worthless gifts. When I swear true loyalty to her, she taunts me with my betrayal of my friend. When I offer my vows to her beauty, she tells me to remember how I broke my oath when I broke faith with Julia, whom I loved. And in spite of all her sharp retorts, the least of which would kill a lover's hope, my love, like a spaniel, grows the more she kicks it away, and goes on fawning on her. But here comes Thurio. Now we must go to her window and play her some evening music.
How now, Sir Proteus, are you crept before us?
Well, Sir Proteus, have you crept here before us?
Ay, gentle Thurio, for you know that love / Will creep in service where it cannot go.
Yes, gentle Thurio, because you know that love will creep to serve where it can't walk.
Ay, but I hope, sir, that you love not here.
Yes, but I hope, sir, that you don't love here.
Sir, but I do, or else I would be hence.
But I do, sir, or else I wouldn't be here.
I thank you for your own. Now, gentlemen, / Let's tune, and to it lustily awhile.
Thank you for yours. Now, gentlemen, let's tune up and play heartily for a while.
Now, my young guest, methinks you're allycholly. I pray you, why is it?
Now, my young guest, I think you're melancholy. Please tell me, why is that?
Marry, mine host, because I cannot be merry.
Well, landlord, because I can't be merry.
Come, we'll have you merry. I'll bring you where you shall hear music, / and see the gentleman that you asked for.
Come on, we'll make you merry. I'll take you where you'll hear music and see the gentleman you asked about.
But shall I hear him speak?
But will I hear him speak?
That will be music to me.
Yes; but quiet, let's hear them.

Who is Silvia? What is she, / That all our swains commend her? / Holy, fair, and wise is she; / The heaven such grace did lend her, / That she might admired be. / Is she kind as she is fair? / For beauty lives with kindness. / Love doth to her eyes repair, / To help him of his blindness; / And, being helped, inhabits there. / Then to Silvia let us sing, / That Silvia is excelling; / She excels each mortal thing / Upon the dull earth dwelling. / To her let us garlands bring.

Who is Silvia, and what is she, that all our young men praise her? She is holy, beautiful and wise; heaven gave her such grace so that she would be admired. Is she as kind as she is beautiful? Beauty lives with kindness. Love, who is blind, goes to her eyes to be cured of his blindness, and once cured, he lives there. So let us sing to Silvia that she is supreme. She surpasses every mortal thing that lives on this dull earth. Let us bring her garlands.
How now, are you sadder than you were before? / How do you, man? The music likes you not.
What's this, are you sadder than you were before? What's the matter, man? Don't you like the music?
You mistake; the musician likes me not.
You've got it wrong; it's the musician who doesn't like me.
How, out of tune on the strings?
What, out of tune on the strings?
Not so; but yet so false that he grieves my very heart-strings.
Not that; but so false that he hurts my very heartstrings.
Ay, I would I were deaf; it makes me have a slow heart.
Yes, I wish I were deaf; it makes my heart heavy.
I perceive you delight not in music.
I can see you don't enjoy music.
Not a whit, when it jars so.
Not a bit, when it's so out of tune.
Hark, what fine change is in the music!
Listen, what a lovely change of key in the music!
Ay, that change is the spite.
Yes, that change is what hurts.
You would have them always play but one thing?
You'd like them to play only one thing all the time?
I would always have one play but one thing. / But, host, doth this Sir Proteus, that we talk on, / Often resort unto this gentlewoman?
I'd like one man always to play only one thing. But landlord, does this Sir Proteus we're talking about often visit this lady?
I tell you what Lance, his man, told me: he loved her out of all nick.
I'll tell you what Lance, his servant, told me: he loves her beyond all measure.
Gone to seek his dog, which tomorrow, by his master's command, he must / carry for a present to his lady.
Gone to look for his dog, which his master has told him to take tomorrow as a present to his lady.
Peace, stand aside. The company parts.
Quiet, stand aside. The group is breaking up.
Sir Thurio, fear not you; I will so plead / That you shall say my cunning drift excels.
Don't worry, Sir Thurio. I'll plead for you so well that you'll say my clever plan is brilliant.
Madam, good even to your ladyship.
Madam, good evening to your ladyship.
I thank you for your music, gentlemen. / Who is that that spake?
Thank you for your music, gentlemen. Who was that who spoke?
One, lady, if you knew his pure heart's truth, / You would quickly learn to know him by his voice.
Someone, lady, whom you'd quickly learn to recognise by his voice, if you knew how true his heart is.
Sir Proteus, as I take it.
Sir Proteus, gentle lady, and your servant.
Sir Proteus, gentle lady, and your servant.

You have your wish. My will is even this, / That presently you hie you home to bed. / Thou subtle, perjured, false, disloyal man, / Think'st thou I am so shallow, so conceitless, / To be seduced by thy flattery, / That hast deceived so many with thy vows? / Return, return, and make thy love amends. / For me, by this pale queen of night I swear, / I am so far from granting thy request / That I despise thee for thy wrongful suit, / And by and by intend to chide myself / Even for this time I spend in talking to thee.

You have your wish. What I want is this: that you go home to bed at once. You sly, lying, false, disloyal man, do you think I'm so shallow, so stupid, that I'll be seduced by your flattery, when you've deceived so many with your vows? Go back, go back, and make it up to your love. As for me, I swear by this pale moon that I'm so far from granting your request that I despise you for your wicked courting, and in a moment I'll scold myself for even the time I'm spending talking to you.
I grant, sweet love, that I did love a lady, / But she is dead.
I admit, sweet love, that I did love a lady, but she's dead.
[Aside] 'Twere false, if I should speak it, / For I am sure she is not buried.
[Aside] That would be a lie if I said it, because I'm sure she's not buried.
Say that she be; yet Valentine thy friend / Survives, to whom, thyself art witness, / I am betrothed. And art thou not ashamed / To wrong him with thy importunacy?
Suppose she is; still, your friend Valentine is alive, and as you yourself know, I'm engaged to him. Aren't you ashamed to wrong him by pestering me?
I likewise hear that Valentine is dead.
I've also heard that Valentine is dead.
And so suppose am I, for in his grave, / Assure thyself, my love is buried.
Then suppose I am too, because, believe me, my love is buried in his grave.
Sweet lady, let me rake it from the earth.
Sweet lady, let me dig it up from the earth.
Go to thy lady's grave and call hers thence, / Or, at the least, in hers sepulchre thine.
Go to your lady's grave and call her love out of it, or at least bury yours in hers.

Madam, if your heart be so obdurate, / Vouchsafe me yet your picture for my love, / The picture that is hanging in your chamber; / To that I'll speak, to that I'll sigh and weep; / For since the substance of your perfect self / Is else devoted, I am but a shadow; / And to your shadow will I make true love.

Madam, if your heart is so hard, at least grant me your picture for my love, the picture that hangs in your room. I'll speak to it, sigh and weep to it. Because since the real substance of your perfect self belongs to someone else, I'm only a shadow, and I'll make true love to your shadow.
[Aside] If 'twere a substance you would sure deceive it / And make it but a shadow, as I am.
[Aside] If it were a real person, you'd surely deceive it and make it only a shadow, as I am.
I am very loath to be your idol, sir; / But since your falsehood shall become you well / To worship shadows and adore false shapes, / Send to me in the morning, and I'll send it. / And so, good rest.
I very much dislike being your idol, sir; but since it suits your falseness to worship shadows and adore false images, send for it in the morning and I'll send it to you. And so, good night.
As wretches have o'ernight / That wait for execution in the morn.
The kind of night a wretch has, waiting to be executed in the morning.
By my halidom, I was fast asleep.
By my holy relics, I was fast asleep.
Pray you, where lies Sir Proteus?
Tell me, where is Sir Proteus staying?
Marry, at my house. Trust me, I think 'tis almost day.
Why, at my inn. Believe me, I think it's almost daybreak.
Not so; but it hath been the longest night / That e'er I watched, and the most heaviest.
Not yet; but it's been the longest night I've ever stayed awake through, and the saddest.
This is the hour that Madam Silvia / Entreated me to call and know her mind; / There's some great matter she'd employ me in. / Madam, madam!
This is the time Madam Silvia asked me to come and find out what she wants. There's some important business she wants me for. Madam, madam!
Your servant and your friend; / One that attends your ladyship's command.
Your servant and your friend; someone who waits on your ladyship's orders.
Sir Eglamour, a thousand times good morrow.
Sir Eglamour, a thousand good mornings.
As many, worthy lady, to yourself. / According to your ladyship's impose, / I am thus early come to know what service / It is your pleasure to command me in.
As many to you, worthy lady. As your ladyship ordered, I've come this early to find out what service you'd like me to do.

O Eglamour, thou art a gentleman— / Think not I flatter, for I swear I do not— / Valiant, wise, remorseful, well accomplished. / Thou art not ignorant what dear good will / I bear unto the banished Valentine, / Nor how my father would enforce me marry / Vain Thurio, whom my very soul abhorred. / Thyself hast loved, and I have heard thee say / No grief did ever come so near thy heart / As when thy lady and thy true love died, / Upon whose grave thou vowed'st pure chastity. / Sir Eglamour, I would to Valentine, / To Mantua, where I hear he makes abode; / And for the ways are dangerous to pass, / I do desire thy worthy company, / Upon whose faith and honour I repose. / Urge not my father's anger, Eglamour, / But think upon my grief, a lady's grief, / And on the justice of my flying hence / To keep me from a most unholy match, / Which heaven and fortune still rewards with plagues. / I do desire thee, even from a heart / As full of sorrows as the sea of sands, / To bear me company and go with me; / If not, to hide what I have said to thee, / That I may venture to depart alone.

Oh, Eglamour, you're a gentleman, and don't think I'm flattering you, because I swear I'm not: brave, wise, compassionate, accomplished. You know how much I love the banished Valentine, and how my father would force me to marry foolish Thurio, whom I hate with all my soul. You've loved yourself, and I've heard you say no grief ever cut so close to your heart as when your lady, your true love, died, and you vowed on her grave to live chaste for ever. Sir Eglamour, I want to go to Valentine, to Mantua, where I hear he's living. And since the roads are dangerous to travel, I'd like your worthy company, because I trust your loyalty and honour. Don't remind me of my father's anger, Eglamour. Think of my grief, a lady's grief, and how right I am to run away from here to escape a most unholy marriage, which heaven and fortune always punish with misery. I beg you, from a heart as full of sorrows as the sea is of sand, keep me company and come with me. If not, keep secret what I've told you, so that I can risk going alone.

Madam, I pity much your grievances, / Which, since I know they virtuously are placed, / I give consent to go along with you, / Recking as little what betideth me / As much I wish all good befortune you. / When will you go?

Madam, I feel deeply for your troubles, and since I know your feelings are honourable, I agree to go with you, caring as little about what happens to me as I wish for good things to happen to you. When will you go?
At Friar Patrick's cell, / Where I intend holy confession.
At Friar Patrick's cell, where I mean to go to confession.
I will not fail your ladyship. Good morrow, gentle lady.
I won't let your ladyship down. Good morning, gentle lady.

When a man's servant shall play the cur with him, look you, it goes / hard: one that I brought up of a puppy; one that I saved from drowning / when three or four of his blind brothers and sisters went to it. I have / taught him even as one would say precisely, "Thus I would teach a dog." / I was sent to deliver him as a present to Mistress Silvia from my / master; and I came no sooner into the dining-chamber but he steps me to / her trencher and steals her capon's leg. O, 'tis a foul thing when a / cur cannot keep himself in all companies! I would have, as one should / say, one that takes upon him to be a dog indeed, to be, as it were, a / dog at all things. If I had not had more wit than he, to take a fault / upon me that he did, I think verily he had been hanged for't; sure as I / live, he had suffered for't. You shall judge. He thrusts me himself / into the company of three or four gentleman-like dogs under the Duke's / table; he had not been there—bless the mark!—a pissing-while but all / the chamber smelt him. "Out with the dog!" says one; "What cur is / that?" says another; "Whip him out", says the third; "Hang him up", / says the Duke. I, having been acquainted with the smell before, knew it / was Crab, and goes me to the fellow that whips the dogs. "Friend," / quoth I, "you mean to whip the dog?" "Ay, marry do I," quoth he. "You do / him the more wrong," quoth I. "'Twas I did the thing you wot of." He / makes me no more ado but whips me out of the chamber. How many masters / would do this for his servant? Nay, I'll be sworn I have sat in the / stock for puddings he hath stolen, otherwise he had been executed. I / have stood on the pillory for geese he hath killed, otherwise he had / suffered for't. [To Crab] Thou think'st not of this now. Nay, I / remember the trick you served me when I took my leave of Madam Silvia. / Did not I bid thee still mark me, and do as I do? When didst thou see / me heave up my leg and make water against a gentlewoman's farthingale? / Didst thou ever see me do such a trick?

When a man's servant behaves like a cur to him, you see, it's hard: one I brought up from a puppy, one I saved from drowning when three or four of his blind brothers and sisters went that way. I've trained him exactly as you'd say, "That's how I'd train a dog." I was sent to give him as a present to Mistress Silvia from my master, and I'd hardly got into the dining room before he trots up to her plate and steals her chicken leg. Oh, it's a terrible thing when a dog can't behave himself in company! I'd want one that took it on himself to be a real dog, a dog, so to speak, at everything. If I hadn't had more sense than him and taken the blame for something he did, I truly think he'd have been hanged for it; as sure as I'm alive, he'd have paid for it. You can judge for yourselves. He pushes in among three or four gentlemanly dogs under the Duke's table, and he hadn't been there, excuse me, long enough to have a pee before the whole room could smell him. "Out with the dog!" says one; "What mutt is that?" says another; "Whip him out," says a third; "Hang him," says the Duke. I knew the smell already, so I knew it was Crab, and I go up to the fellow who whips the dogs. "Friend," I say, "are you going to whip the dog?" "Yes, I certainly am," he says. "Then you do him all the more wrong," I say. "It was me who did the thing you know about." Without more fuss he whips me out of the room. How many masters would do that for their servant? No, I swear I've sat in the stocks for puddings he's stolen, or else he'd have been executed. I've stood in the pillory for geese he's killed, or else he'd have suffered for it. [To Crab] You don't think about that now. No, I remember the trick you played on me when I said goodbye to Madam Silvia. Didn't I tell you always to watch me and do as I do? When did you ever see me lift my leg and pee against a lady's hooped skirt? Did you ever see me do a trick like that?
Sebastian is thy name? I like thee well, / And will employ thee in some service presently.
Your name is Sebastian? I like you very much, and I'll give you some work to do right away.
In what you please; I'll do what I can.
Whatever you like; I'll do what I can.
I hope thou wilt. [To Lance] How now, you whoreson peasant, / Where have you been these two days loitering?
I hope you will. [To Lance] Well, you son-of-a-whore peasant, where have you been loafing these two days?
Marry, sir, I carried Mistress Silvia the dog you bade me.
Why, sir, I took Mistress Silvia the dog you told me to.
And what says she to my little jewel?
And what does she say about my little jewel?
Marry, she says your dog was a cur, and tells you currish thanks is / good enough for such a present.
Well, she says your dog was a mutt, and that a dog's thanks is good enough for a present like that.
No, indeed, did she not. Here have I brought him back again.
No, she certainly didn't. I've brought him back here.
What, didst thou offer her this from me?
What, did you offer her this one from me?
Ay, sir, the other squirrel was stolen from me by the hangman's boys in / the market-place, and then I offered her mine own, who is a dog as big / as ten of yours, and therefore the gift the greater.
Yes, sir. The other little squirrel of a dog was stolen from me by the hangman's boys in the market square, and then I offered her my own, who's a dog as big as ten of yours, and so a bigger present.
Go, get thee hence, and find my dog again, / Or ne'er return again into my sight. / Away, I say. Stayest thou to vex me here? / A slave that still an end turns me to shame.
Go on, get out of here and find my dog, or never come into my sight again. Go, I say. Are you staying here to annoy me? A slave who always brings me shame.

Sebastian, I have entertained thee / Partly that I have need of such a youth / That can with some discretion do my business— / For 'tis no trusting to yond foolish lout— / But chiefly for thy face and thy behaviour, / Which, if my augury deceive me not, / Witness good bringing up, fortune, and truth. / Therefore, know thou, for this I entertain thee. / Go presently, and take this ring with thee, / Deliver it to Madam Silvia. / She loved me well delivered it to me.

Sebastian, I've taken you on partly because I need a young man like you who can do my business with some discretion, since there's no trusting that foolish oaf; but mainly because of your face and your manner, which, if my judgement isn't wrong, show a good upbringing, good fortune and honesty. So know that this is why I'm employing you. Go at once and take this ring with you. Give it to Madam Silvia. The woman who gave it to me loved me very much.
It seems you loved not her, to leave her token. / She's dead belike?
It seems you didn't love her, if you're giving away her keepsake. Is she dead, perhaps?
Not so; I think she lives.
I cannot choose / But pity her.

Because methinks that she loved you as well / As you do love your lady Silvia. / She dreams on him that has forgot her love; / You dote on her that cares not for your love. / 'Tis pity love should be so contrary; / And thinking on it makes me cry "Alas."

Because I think she loved you as much as you love your lady Silvia. She dreams of the man who has forgotten her love; you dote on the woman who cares nothing for yours. It's a pity love should be so contrary, and thinking about it makes me cry "Oh dear."

Well, give her that ring, and therewithal / This letter. That's her chamber. Tell my lady / I claim the promise for her heavenly picture. / Your message done, hie home unto my chamber, / Where thou shalt find me sad and solitary.

Well, give her that ring, and this letter with it. That's her room. Tell my lady I'm claiming the heavenly picture she promised me. When you've delivered your message, hurry home to my room, where you'll find me sad and alone.

How many women would do such a message? / Alas, poor Proteus, thou hast entertained / A fox to be the shepherd of thy lambs. / Alas, poor fool, why do I pity him / That with his very heart despiseth me? / Because he loves her, he despiseth me; / Because I love him, I must pity him. / This ring I gave him when he parted from me, / To bind him to remember my good will; / And now am I, unhappy messenger, / To plead for that which I would not obtain, / To carry that which I would have refused, / To praise his faith, which I would have dispraised. / I am my master's true confirmed love, / But cannot be true servant to my master / Unless I prove false traitor to myself. / Yet will I woo for him, but yet so coldly / As, heaven it knows, I would not have him speed.

How many women would carry a message like this? Oh, poor Proteus, you've hired a fox to look after your lambs. Oh, you poor fool, why do I pity him, when he despises me with all his heart? Because he loves her, he despises me; because I love him, I have to pity him. I gave him this ring when he left me, to make him remember my love; and now I, an unhappy messenger, have to plead for something I don't want him to get, carry something I'd like to see refused, and praise his faithfulness, which I'd like to criticise. I'm my master's true and constant love, but I can't be a true servant to my master without being a false traitor to myself. Still, I'll woo her for him, but so half-heartedly that, heaven knows, I don't want him to succeed.
Gentlewoman, good day. I pray you be my mean / To bring me where to speak with Madam Silvia.
Good day, lady. Please help me find where I can speak with Madam Silvia.
What would you with her, if that I be she?
What do you want with her, if I'm she?
If you be she, I do entreat your patience / To hear me speak the message I am sent on.
If you are, please be patient and hear the message I've been sent with.
From my master, Sir Proteus, madam.
From my master, Sir Proteus, madam.
O, he sends you for a picture?
Oh, he's sent you for a picture?
Go, give your master this. Tell him from me, / One Julia, that his changing thoughts forget, / Would better fit his chamber than this shadow.
Go and give your master this. Tell him from me that a certain Julia, whom his fickle mind forgets, would suit his room better than this shadow.
Madam, please you peruse this letter.
Pardon me, madam, I have unadvised / Delivered you a paper that I should not. / This is the letter to your ladyship.
Forgive me, madam, I've carelessly given you a paper I shouldn't have. This is the letter to your ladyship.
I pray thee, let me look on that again.
Please, let me look at that one again.
It may not be. Good madam, pardon me.
I can't, good madam. Forgive me.
There, hold. / I will not look upon your master's lines. / I know they are stuffed with protestations / And full of new-found oaths, which he will break / As easily as I do tear his paper.
There, take it. I won't look at your master's writing. I know it's stuffed with declarations and full of new oaths, which he'll break as easily as I tear up his paper.
Madam, he sends your ladyship this ring.
Madam, he sends your ladyship this ring.

The more shame for him that he sends it me; / For I have heard him say a thousand times / His Julia gave it him at his departure. / Though his false finger have profaned the ring, / Mine shall not do his Julia so much wrong.

All the more shame to him for sending it to me, because I've heard him say a thousand times that his Julia gave it to him when he left. Though his false finger has dishonoured the ring, mine won't do his Julia such a wrong.
I thank you, madam, that you tender her. / Poor gentlewoman, my master wrongs her much.
I thank you, madam, for being kind to her. Poor lady, my master wrongs her badly.
Almost as well as I do know myself. / To think upon her woes, I do protest / That I have wept a hundred several times.
Almost as well as I know myself. I swear I've wept a hundred times thinking about her troubles.
Belike she thinks that Proteus hath forsook her?
I suppose she thinks Proteus has abandoned her?
I think she doth, and that's her cause of sorrow.
I think she does, and that's the cause of her sorrow.

She hath been fairer, madam, than she is. / When she did think my master loved her well, / She, in my judgement, was as fair as you. / But since she did neglect her looking-glass / And threw her sun-expelling mask away, / The air hath starved the roses in her cheeks / And pinched the lily-tincture of her face, / That now she is become as black as I.

She has been more beautiful than she is now, madam. When she believed my master loved her, she was, in my opinion, as beautiful as you. But since she stopped looking in her mirror and threw away the mask that kept off the sun, the weather has withered the roses in her cheeks and shrivelled the lily-white of her face, so that now she's become as brown as I am.

About my stature; for at Pentecost, / When all our pageants of delight were played, / Our youth got me to play the woman's part, / And I was trimmed in Madam Julia's gown, / Which served me as fit, by all men's judgements, / As if the garment had been made for me; / Therefore I know she is about my height. / And at that time I made her weep agood, / For I did play a lamentable part. / Madam, 'twas Ariadne, passioning / For Theseus' perjury and unjust flight, / Which I so lively acted with my tears / That my poor mistress, moved therewithal, / Wept bitterly; and would I might be dead / If I in thought felt not her very sorrow.

About my height. At Whitsun, when all our entertainments were put on, the young people got me to play the woman's part, and I was dressed in Madam Julia's gown, which everyone said fitted me as well as if it had been made for me. So I know she's about my height. And that time I made her cry her heart out, because I played a sad part. Madam, it was Ariadne, grieving over Theseus's broken vows and his cruel desertion. I acted it so vividly with my tears that my poor mistress was moved and wept bitterly; and I wish I may die if I didn't feel her sorrow in my own heart.

She is beholding to thee, gentle youth. / Alas, poor lady, desolate and left! / I weep myself to think upon thy words. / Here, youth, there is my purse. I give thee this / For thy sweet mistress' sake, because thou lov'st her. / Farewell.

She owes you a lot, gentle youth. Oh, poor lady, deserted and alone! It makes me cry myself to think about what you've said. Here, young man, here's my purse. I give you this for your sweet mistress's sake, because you love her. Goodbye.
And she shall thank you for't, if e'er you know her.
And she'll thank you for it, if you ever meet her.

A virtuous gentlewoman, mild and beautiful. / I hope my master's suit will be but cold, / Since she respects my mistress' love so much. / Alas, how love can trifle with itself! / Here is her picture; let me see. I think / If I had such a tire, this face of mine / Were full as lovely as is this of hers; / And yet the painter flattered her a little, / Unless I flatter with myself too much. / Her hair is auburn, mine is perfect yellow; / If that be all the difference in his love, / I'll get me such a coloured periwig. / Her eyes are grey as glass, and so are mine. / Ay, but her forehead's low, and mine's as high. / What should it be that he respects in her / But I can make respective in myself, / If this fond Love were not a blinded god? / Come, shadow, come, and take this shadow up, / For 'tis thy rival. O thou senseless form, / Thou shalt be worshipped, kissed, loved, and adored; / And were there sense in his idolatry, / My substance should be statue in thy stead. / I'll use thee kindly for thy mistress' sake, / That used me so; or else, by Jove I vow, / I should have scratched out your unseeing eyes / To make my master out of love with thee.

A virtuous lady, gentle and beautiful. I hope my master's wooing gets nowhere, since she cares so much about my mistress's love. Oh, how love can play games with itself! Here's her picture; let me look. I think if I had a headdress like that, this face of mine would be every bit as lovely as hers. And yet the painter flattered her a little, unless I'm flattering myself too much. Her hair is auburn; mine is perfectly golden. If that's the only difference in his love, I'll get myself a wig that colour. Her eyes are as grey as glass, and so are mine. Yes, but her forehead is low, and mine is high. What can it be that he values in her that I couldn't make him value in me, if foolish Love weren't a blind god? Come, shadow, come and pick up this shadow, because it's your rival. Oh, you unfeeling image, you'll be worshipped, kissed, loved and adored; and if there were any sense in his idolatry, my real self would be the statue in your place. I'll treat you kindly for your mistress's sake, since she treated me kindly; or else, I swear by Jove, I'd have scratched out your unseeing eyes to make my master fall out of love with you.

The sun begins to gild the western sky, / And now it is about the very hour / That Silvia at Friar Patrick's cell should meet me. / She will not fail, for lovers break not hours, / Unless it be to come before their time, / So much they spur their expedition.

The sun is beginning to turn the western sky gold, and now it's just about the hour when Silvia should meet me at Friar Patrick's cell. She won't fail, because lovers don't miss appointments, unless it's to come early, they're in such a hurry.
See where she comes. Lady, a happy evening!
Look, here she comes. Lady, a happy evening!
Amen, amen. Go on, good Eglamour, / Out at the postern by the abbey wall. / I fear I am attended by some spies.
Amen to that. Lead on, good Eglamour, out through the back gate by the abbey wall. I'm afraid I'm being followed by spies.
Fear not. The forest is not three leagues off; / If we recover that, we are sure enough.
Don't worry. The forest is less than three leagues away. If we get there, we're safe enough.
Sir Proteus, what says Silvia to my suit?
Sir Proteus, what does Silvia say to my courtship?
O, sir, I find her milder than she was, / And yet she takes exceptions at your person.
Oh, sir, I find her gentler than she was, and yet she objects to your appearance.
What? That my leg is too long?
What? That my leg is too long?
No, that it is too little.
I'll wear a boot to make it somewhat rounder.
I'll wear a boot to make it a bit rounder.
[Aside] But love will not be spurred to what it loathes.
[Aside] But you can't spur love towards something it hates.
What says she to my face?
What does she say about my face?
She says it is a fair one.
She says it's a fair one.
Nay, then, the wanton lies; my face is black.
No, then the flirt is lying; my face is dark.
But pearls are fair; and the old saying is, / "Black men are pearls in beauteous ladies' eyes."
But pearls are fair, and the old saying goes, "Dark men are pearls in beautiful ladies' eyes."
[Aside] 'Tis true, such pearls as put out ladies' eyes, / For I had rather wink than look on them.
[Aside] That's true: the kind of pearls, cataracts, that blind ladies' eyes, because I'd rather shut my eyes than look at them.
How does she like my conversation?
Ill, when you talk of war.
Badly, when you talk about war.
But well when I discourse of love and peace.
But well when I talk about love and peace.
[Aside] But better, indeed, when you hold your peace.
[Aside] But better, actually, when you hold your peace.
What says she to my valour?
What does she say about my courage?
O, sir, she makes no doubt of that.
Oh, sir, she has no doubt about that.
[Aside] She needs not, when she knows it cowardice.
[Aside] She doesn't need any, when she knows it's cowardice.
What says she to my birth?
What does she say about my birth?
[Aside] True, from a gentleman to a fool.
[Aside] True: descended from a gentleman to a fool.
Does she think about my estates?
Oh yes, and she pities them.
[Aside] That such an ass should owe them.
[Aside] Because such an ass owns them.
That they are out by lease.
Because they're let out on lease.
How now, Sir Proteus! How now, Thurio! / Which of you saw Sir Eglamour of late?
Well, Sir Proteus! Well, Thurio! Which of you has seen Sir Eglamour lately?

Why then, she's fled unto that peasant Valentine, / And Eglamour is in her company. / 'Tis true, for Friar Lawrence met them both / As he in penance wandered through the forest; / Him he knew well, and guessed that it was she, / But, being masked, he was not sure of it. / Besides, she did intend confession / At Patrick's cell this even, and there she was not. / These likelihoods confirm her flight from hence. / Therefore, I pray you, stand not to discourse, / But mount you presently and meet with me / Upon the rising of the mountain foot / That leads toward Mantua, whither they are fled. / Dispatch, sweet gentlemen, and follow me.

Why then, she's run off to that peasant Valentine, and Eglamour is with her. It's true, because Friar Lawrence met them both as he was wandering through the forest doing penance. He knew Eglamour well and guessed it was her, but because she was masked he wasn't sure. Besides, she meant to go to confession at Patrick's cell this evening, and she wasn't there. These signs confirm that she's run away from here. So please don't stand here talking, but mount your horses at once and meet me at the foot of the hills on the road to Mantua, where they've fled. Hurry, sweet gentlemen, and follow me.
Why, this it is to be a peevish girl / That flies her fortune when it follows her. / I'll after, more to be revenged on Eglamour / Than for the love of reckless Silvia.
Why, this is what it is to be a contrary girl, who runs away from good fortune when it follows her. I'll go after her, more to get revenge on Eglamour than for love of reckless Silvia.
And I will follow, more for Silvia's love / Than hate of Eglamour that goes with her.
And I'll follow, more for love of Silvia than hatred of Eglamour, who's gone with her.
And I will follow, more to cross that love / Than hate for Silvia, that is gone for love.
And I'll follow, more to block that love than out of hatred for Silvia, who's gone for love.
Come, come, be patient. We must bring you to our captain.
Come on, come on, be patient. We have to take you to our captain.
A thousand more mischances than this one / Have learned me how to brook this patiently.
A thousand worse misfortunes than this one have taught me to bear it patiently.
Where is the gentleman that was with her?
Where's the gentleman who was with her?

Being nimble-footed, he hath outrun us. / But Moyses and Valerius follow him. / Go thou with her to the west end of the wood; / There is our captain. We'll follow him that's fled. / The thicket is beset; he cannot 'scape.

He was quick on his feet and outran us. But Moyses and Valerius are after him. You take her to the west end of the wood; our captain is there. We'll follow the one who ran. The thicket is surrounded; he can't escape.
Come, I must bring you to our captain's cave. / Fear not; he bears an honourable mind / And will not use a woman lawlessly.
Come, I have to take you to our captain's cave. Don't be afraid. He's an honourable man and won't treat a woman lawlessly.
O Valentine, this I endure for thee!
