Oh, Valentine, I'm going through this for you!

How use doth breed a habit in a man! / This shadowy desert, unfrequented woods, / I better brook than flourishing peopled towns. / Here can I sit alone, unseen of any, / And to the nightingale's complaining notes / Tune my distresses and record my woes. / O thou that dost inhabit in my breast, / Leave not the mansion so long tenantless, / Lest, growing ruinous, the building fall / And leave no memory of what it was. / Repair me with thy presence, Silvia; / Thou gentle nymph, cherish thy forlorn swain.

How custom turns into habit in a man! I like this shady wilderness, these lonely woods, better than busy, crowded towns. Here I can sit alone, seen by no one, and match my troubles to the nightingale's sad song and sing out my sorrows. Oh, you who live in my heart, don't leave the house empty for so long, in case it falls into ruin, collapses and leaves no memory of what it was. Rebuild me with your presence, Silvia. Gentle nymph, comfort your lonely shepherd.

What hallowing and what stir is this today? / These are my mates, that make their wills their law, / Have some unhappy passenger in chase. / They love me well; yet I have much to do / To keep them from uncivil outrages. / Withdraw thee, Valentine. Who's this comes here?

What shouting and commotion is this today? It's my companions, who make their own wishes their law, chasing some unlucky traveller. They love me well, yet I have a hard job keeping them from savage outrages. Step aside, Valentine. Who's this coming here?

Madam, this service I have done for you— / Though you respect not aught your servant doth— / To hazard life, and rescue you from him / That would have forced your honour and your love. / Vouchsafe me for my meed but one fair look; / A smaller boon than this I cannot beg, / And less than this, I am sure, you cannot give.

Madam, I've done you this service, though you care nothing for anything your servant does: I've risked my life to rescue you from the man who would have taken your honour and your love by force. As my reward, grant me just one kind look. I can't ask for a smaller favour than this, and I'm sure you can't give less.
[Aside] How like a dream is this I see and hear! / Love, lend me patience to forbear awhile.
[Aside] This is like a dream, what I'm seeing and hearing! Love, give me patience to hold back a while.
O miserable, unhappy that I am!
Oh, how wretched and unhappy I am!
Unhappy were you, madam, ere I came; / But by my coming I have made you happy.
You were unhappy, madam, before I came; but by coming I've made you happy.
By thy approach thou mak'st me most unhappy.
By coming near me you make me most unhappy.
[Aside] And me, when he approacheth to your presence.
[Aside] And me, when he comes near you.

Had I been seized by a hungry lion, / I would have been a breakfast to the beast / Rather than have false Proteus rescue me. / O heaven, be judge how I love Valentine, / Whose life's as tender to me as my soul! / And full as much, for more there cannot be, / I do detest false perjured Proteus. / Therefore be gone, solicit me no more.

If I'd been caught by a hungry lion, I would rather have been the beast's breakfast than have false Proteus rescue me. Oh, heaven, judge how much I love Valentine, whose life is as dear to me as my soul! And just as much, since there can't be more, I hate false, oath-breaking Proteus. So go away, and stop pestering me.
What dangerous action, stood it next to death, / Would I not undergo for one calm look! / O, 'tis the curse in love, and still approved, / When women cannot love where they're beloved.
What dangerous deed, even one that came close to death, wouldn't I undertake for one gentle look! Oh, it's the curse of love, and always proved true, when women can't love where they are loved.

When Proteus cannot love where he's beloved. / Read over Julia's heart, thy first best love, / For whose dear sake thou didst then rend thy faith / Into a thousand oaths; and all those oaths / Descended into perjury to love me. / Thou hast no faith left now, unless thou'dst two, / And that's far worse than none; better have none / Than plural faith, which is too much by one. / Thou counterfeit to thy true friend!

When Proteus can't love where he's loved. Read Julia's heart again, your first and best love, for whose dear sake you tore your loyalty into a thousand oaths; and all those oaths sank into lies when you loved me. You have no faith left now, unless you have two, and that's far worse than none. Better to have none than a double faith, which is one too many. You fake, to your true friend!
In love, who cares about a friend?
Nay, if the gentle spirit of moving words / Can no way change you to a milder form, / I'll woo you like a soldier, at arms' end, / And love you 'gainst the nature of love—force ye.
No, if the gentle power of moving words can't soften you at all, I'll woo you like a soldier, with weapons, and love you against the nature of love: I'll force you.
I'll force thee yield to my desire.
I'll force you to give in to my desire.
[Comes forward] Ruffian, let go that rude uncivil touch, / Thou friend of an ill fashion!
[Comes forward] Thug, let go of her, that's a brutal, savage touch, you false kind of friend!

Thou common friend, that's without faith or love, / For such is a friend now. Treacherous man, / Thou hast beguiled my hopes; nought but mine eye / Could have persuaded me. Now I dare not say / I have one friend alive; thou wouldst disprove me. / Who should be trusted, when one's right hand / Is perjured to the bosom? Proteus, / I am sorry I must never trust thee more, / But count the world a stranger for thy sake. / The private wound is deepest. O time most accurst, / 'Mongst all foes that a friend should be the worst!

You worthless friend, without loyalty or love, because that's what friends are like now. Treacherous man, you've cheated my hopes. Nothing but my own eyes could have convinced me. Now I don't dare say I have one friend alive; you'd prove me wrong. Who can be trusted, when your own right hand betrays your heart? Proteus, I'm sorry that I must never trust you again, but treat the whole world as a stranger because of you. The private wound is the deepest. Oh, most cursed time, that of all enemies a friend should be the worst!
My shame and guilt confounds me. / Forgive me, Valentine; if hearty sorrow / Be a sufficient ransom for offence, / I tender 't here. I do as truly suffer / As e'er I did commit.
My shame and guilt overwhelm me. Forgive me, Valentine. If heartfelt sorrow is enough to pay for the wrong, I offer it here. I suffer as truly as I ever sinned.

Then I am paid, / And once again I do receive thee honest. / Who by repentance is not satisfied / Is nor of heaven nor earth, for these are pleased; / By penitence th' Eternal's wrath's appeased. / And that my love may appear plain and free, / All that was mine in Silvia I give thee.

Then I'm repaid, and once again I accept you as an honest man. Anyone who isn't satisfied by repentance belongs neither to heaven nor earth, because they are both satisfied by it; repentance calms even God's anger. And so that my love for you is plain and generous, I give you everything that was mine in Silvia.
Why, boy! / Why, wag! How now? What's the matter? Look up; speak.
Why, boy! Why, lad! What's this? What's the matter? Look up; speak.
O good sir, my master charged me to deliver a ring to Madam Silvia, / which out of my neglect was never done.
Oh, good sir, my master told me to deliver a ring to Madam Silvia, and I carelessly never did it.
Here it is; this is it.
How, let me see. / Why, this is the ring I gave to Julia.
What? Let me see. Why, this is the ring I gave to Julia.
O, cry you mercy, sir, I have mistook. / This is the ring you sent to Silvia.
Oh, I beg your pardon, sir, I've made a mistake. This is the ring you sent to Silvia.
But how cam'st thou by this ring? At my depart / I gave this unto Julia.
But how did you get this ring? When I left, I gave it to Julia.
And Julia herself did give it me, / And Julia herself have brought it hither.
And Julia herself gave it to me, and Julia herself has brought it here.

Behold her that gave aim to all thy oaths / And entertained 'em deeply in her heart. / How oft hast thou with perjury cleft the root! / O Proteus, let this habit make thee blush. / Be thou ashamed that I have took upon me / Such an immodest raiment, if shame live / In a disguise of love. / It is the lesser blot, modesty finds, / Women to change their shapes than men their minds.

Look at the woman who was the target of all your oaths and held them deep in her heart. How often you've split that heart to the root with your lies! Oh, Proteus, let these clothes make you blush. Be ashamed that I've had to put on such immodest clothing, if there can be shame in a disguise put on for love. Modesty finds it a smaller stain for women to change their appearance than for men to change their minds.

Than men their minds! 'Tis true. O heaven, were man / But constant, he were perfect. That one error / Fills him with faults, makes him run through all th' sins; / Inconstancy falls off ere it begins. / What is in Silvia's face but I may spy / More fresh in Julia's with a constant eye?

Than men their minds! It's true. Oh heaven, if a man were only constant, he'd be perfect. That one fault fills him with faults and drives him through every sin. Inconstancy gives up before it has properly begun. What is there in Silvia's face that I couldn't see, fresher, in Julia's, with a faithful eye?
Come, come, a hand from either. / Let me be blest to make this happy close. / 'Twere pity two such friends should be long foes.
Come on, come on, a hand from each of you. Let me have the blessing of making this happy ending. It would be a pity for two such friends to be enemies for long.
Bear witness, heaven, I have my wish for ever.
Heaven be my witness, I have what I wish for, for ever.
A prize, a prize, a prize!
A prize, a prize, a prize!
Forbear, forbear, I say! It is my lord the Duke. / Your Grace is welcome to a man disgraced, / Banished Valentine.
Stop, stop, I say! It's my lord the Duke. Your grace is welcome to a disgraced man, the banished Valentine.
Yonder is Silvia, and Silvia's mine.
There's Silvia, and Silvia is mine.

Thurio, give back, or else embrace thy death; / Come not within the measure of my wrath. / Do not name Silvia thine; if once again, / Verona shall not hold thee. Here she stands; / Take but possession of her with a touch— / I dare thee but to breathe upon my love.

Thurio, stand back, or else meet your death. Don't come within reach of my anger. Don't call Silvia yours; if you do it once more, Verona won't be safe for you. Here she stands. Just try to take possession of her with one touch. I dare you even to breathe on my love.
Sir Valentine, I care not for her, I. / I hold him but a fool that will endanger / His body for a girl that loves him not. / I claim her not, and therefore she is thine.
Sir Valentine, I don't care about her, not I. I think anyone's a fool who'd risk his body for a girl who doesn't love him. I give up my claim, so she's yours.

The more degenerate and base art thou / To make such means for her as thou hast done, / And leave her on such slight conditions.— / Now, by the honour of my ancestry, / I do applaud thy spirit, Valentine, / And think thee worthy of an empress' love. / Know then, I here forget all former griefs, / Cancel all grudge, repeal thee home again, / Plead a new state in thy unrivalled merit, / To which I thus subscribe: Sir Valentine, / Thou art a gentleman, and well derived; / Take thou thy Silvia, for thou hast deserved her.

All the more low and contemptible you are, to go to such lengths to win her and then give her up on such easy terms. Now, by the honour of my ancestors, I applaud your spirit, Valentine, and think you worthy of an empress's love. Know, then, that I here forget all my old grievances, cancel every grudge and call you home again. On the strength of your unmatched merit, I declare a new standing for you, and I sign my name to it like this: Sir Valentine, you are a gentleman, and of good birth. Take your Silvia, because you have earned her.
I thank your Grace; the gift hath made me happy. / I now beseech you, for your daughter's sake, / To grant one boon that I shall ask of you.
Thank you, your grace; the gift has made me happy. Now I beg you, for your daughter's sake, to grant one favour I'll ask of you.
I grant it for thine own, whate'er it be.
I grant it for your own sake, whatever it is.

These banished men, that I have kept withal, / Are men endued with worthy qualities. / Forgive them what they have committed here, / And let them be recalled from their exile. / They are reformed, civil, full of good, / And fit for great employment, worthy lord.

These banished men I've lived with are men with good qualities. Forgive them for what they've done here, and let them be called back from exile. They've reformed; they're civilised, full of goodness and fit for important work, worthy lord.
Thou hast prevailed; I pardon them and thee. / Dispose of them as thou know'st their deserts. / Come, let us go; we will include all jars / With triumphs, mirth, and rare solemnity.
You've won; I pardon them and you. Use them as you know they deserve. Come, let's go. We'll end all quarrels with celebrations, merriment and splendid ceremony.
And as we walk along, I dare be bold / With our discourse to make your Grace to smile. / What think you of this page, my lord?
And as we walk along, I'll be bold enough to make your grace smile with our story. What do you think of this page, my lord?
I think the boy hath grace in him; he blushes.
I think the boy has grace in him; he's blushing.
I warrant you, my lord, more grace than boy.
I promise you, my lord, he has more grace than boy in him.
What mean you by that saying?
What do you mean by that?

Please you, I'll tell you as we pass along, / That you will wonder what hath fortuned. / Come, Proteus, 'tis your penance but to hear / The story of your loves discovered. / That done, our day of marriage shall be yours, / One feast, one house, one mutual happiness.

If you please, I'll tell you as we go along, and you'll be amazed at what has happened. Come, Proteus, your only punishment is to hear the story of your loves told in full. After that, our wedding day will be yours too: one feast, one house, one shared happiness.
